quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "But she must have a prize herself, you know," said the Mouse.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Of course," the Dodo replied very gravely. "What else have you got in your pocket?" he went on, turning to Alice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Then they all crowded round her once more, while the Dodo solemnly presented the thimble, saying "We beg your acceptance of this elegant thimble;" and, when it had finished this short speech, they all cheered.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice thought the whole thing very absurd, but they all looked so grave that she did not dare to laugh; and, as she could not think of anything to say, she simply bowed, and took the thimble, looking as solemn as she could.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The next thing was to eat the comfits: this caused some noise and confusion, as the large birds complained that they could not taste theirs, and the small ones choked and had to be patted on the back. However, it was over at last, and they sat down again in a ring, and begged the Mouse to tell them something more.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You promised to tell me your history, you know," said Alice, "and why it is you hate - C and D," she added in a whisper, half afraid that it would be offended again.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Mine is a long and a sad tale!" said the Mouse, turning to Alice, and sighing.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You are not attending!" said the Mouse to Alice severely. "What are you thinking of?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I beg your pardon," said Alice very humbly: "you had got to the fifth bend, I think?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I had not!" cried the Mouse, sharply and very angrily.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "A knot!" said Alice, always ready to make herself useful, and looking anxiously about her. "Oh, do let me help to undo it!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I shall do nothing of the sort," said the Mouse, getting up and walking away. "You insult me by talking such nonsense!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I didn't mean it!" pleaded poor Alice. "But you're so easily offended, you know!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Please come back and finish your story!" Alice called after it; and the others all joined in chorus, "Yes, please do!" but the Mouse only shook its head impatiently, and walked a little quicker.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "What a pity it wouldn't stay!" sighed the Lory, as soon as it was quite out of sight; and an old Crab took the opportunity of saying to her daughter "Ah, my dear! Let this be a lesson to you never to lose your temper!" "Hold your tongue, Ma!" said the young Crab, a little snappishly. "You're enough to try the patience of an oyster!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I wish I had our Dinah here, I know I do!" said Alice aloud, addressing nobody in particular. "She'd soon fetch it back!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And who is Dinah, if I might venture to ask the question?" said the Lory.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice replied eagerly, for she was always ready to talk about her pet: "Dinah's our cat. And she's such a capital one for catching mice you can't think! And oh, I wish you could see her after the birds! Why, she'll eat a little bird as soon as look at it!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This speech caused a remarkable sensation among the party. Some of the birds hurried off at once: one old Magpie began wrapping itself up very carefully, remarking, "I really must be getting home; the night-air doesn't suit my throat!" and a Canary called out in a trembling voice to its children, "Come away, my dears! It's high time you were all in bed!" On various pretexts they all moved off, and Alice was soon left alone.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I wish I hadn't mentioned Dinah!" she said to herself in a melancholy tone. "Nobody seems to like her, down here, and I'm sure she's the best cat in the world! Oh, my dear Dinah! I wonder if I shall ever see you any more!" And here poor Alice began to cry again, for she felt very lonely and low-spirited. In a little while, however, she again heard a little pattering of footsteps in the distance, and she looked up eagerly, half hoping that the Mouse had changed his mind, and was coming back to finish his story.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: It was the White Rabbit, trotting slowly back again, and looking anxiously about as it went, as if it had lost something; and she heard it muttering to itself "The Duchess! The Duchess! Oh my dear paws! Oh my fur and whiskers! She'll get me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets! Where can I have dropped them, I wonder?" Alice guessed in a moment that it was looking for the fan and the pair of white kid gloves, and she very good-naturedly began hunting about for them, but they were nowhere to be seen - everything seemed to have changed since her swim in the pool, and the great hall, with the glass table and the little door, had vanished completely.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Very soon the Rabbit noticed Alice, as she went hunting about, and called out to her in an angry tone, "Why, Mary Ann, what are you doing out here? Run home this moment, and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan! Quick, now!" And Alice was so much frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed to, without trying to explain the mistake it had made.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "He took me for his housemaid," she said to herself as she ran. "How surprised he'll be when he finds out who I am! But I'd better take him his fan and gloves - that is, if I can find them." As she said this, she came upon a neat little house, on the door of which was a bright brass plate with the name "W. RABBIT," engraved upon it. She went in without knocking, and hurried upstairs, in great fear lest she should meet the real Mary Ann, and be turned out of the house before she had found the fan and gloves.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "How queer it seems," Alice said to herself, "to be going messages for a rabbit! I suppose Dinah'll be sending me on messages next!" And she began fancying the sort of thing that would happen: "'Miss Alice! Come here directly, and get ready for your walk!' 'Coming in a minute, nurse! But I've got to see that the mouse doesn't get out.' Only I don't think," Alice went on, "that they'd let Dinah stop in the house if it began ordering people about like that!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: By this time she had found her way into a tidy little room with a table in the window, and on it (as she had hoped) a fan and two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves: she took up the fan and a pair of the gloves, and was just going to leave the room, when her eye fell upon a little bottle that stood near the looking-glass. There was no label this time with the words "DRINK ME," but nevertheless she uncorked it and put it to her lips. "I know something interesting is sure to happen," she said to herself, "whenever I eat or drink anything; so I'll just see what this bottle does. I do hope it'll make me grow large again, for really I'm quite tired of being such a tiny little thing!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: It did so indeed, and much sooner than she had expected: before she had drunk half the bottle, she found her head pressing against the ceiling, and had to stoop to save her neck from being broken. She hastily put down the bottle, saying to herself "That's quite enough - I hope I shan't grow any more - As it is, I can't get out at the door - I do wish I hadn't drunk quite so much!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alas! it was too late to wish that! She went on growing, and growing, and very soon had to kneel down on the floor: in another minute there was not even room for this, and she tried the effect of lying down with one elbow against the door, and the other arm curled round her head. Still she went on growing, and, as a last resource, she put one arm out of the window, and one foot up the chimney, and said to herself "Now I can do no more, whatever happens. What will become of me?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Luckily for Alice, the little magic bottle had now had its full effect, and she grew no larger: still it was very uncomfortable, and, as there seemed to be no sort of chance of her ever getting out of the room again, no wonder she felt unhappy.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It was much pleasanter at home," thought poor Alice, "when one wasn't always growing larger and smaller, and being ordered about by mice and rabbits. I almost wish I hadn't gone down that rabbit-hole - and yet - and yet - it's rather curious, you know, this sort of life! I do wonder what can have happened to me! When I used to read fairy-tales, I fancied that kind of thing never happened, and now here I am in the middle of one! There ought to be a book written about me, that there ought! And when I grow up, I'll write one - but I'm grown up now," she added in a sorrowful tone; "at least there's no room to grow up any more here."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "But then," thought Alice, "shall I never get any older than I am now? That'll be a comfort, one way - never to be an old woman - but then - always to have lessons to learn! Oh, I shouldn't like that!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh, you foolish Alice!" she answered herself. "How can you learn lessons in here? Why, there's hardly room for you, and no room at all for any lesson-books!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: And so she went on, taking first one side and then the other, and making quite a conversation of it altogether; but after a few minutes she heard a voice outside, and stopped to listen.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Mary Ann! Mary Ann!" said the voice. "Fetch me my gloves this moment!" Then came a little pattering of feet on the stairs. Alice knew it was the Rabbit coming to look for her, and she trembled till she shook the house, quite forgetting that she was now about a thousand times as large as the Rabbit, and had no reason to be afraid of it.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Presently the Rabbit came up to the door, and tried to open it; but, as the door opened inwards, and Alice's elbow was pressed hard against it, that attempt proved a failure. Alice heard it say to itself "Then I'll go round and get in at the window."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "That you won't!" thought Alice, and, after waiting till she fancied she heard the Rabbit just under the window, she suddenly spread out her hand, and made a snatch in the air. She did not get hold of anything, but she heard a little shriek and a fall, and a crash of broken glass, from which she concluded that it was just possible it had fallen into a cucumber-frame, or something of the sort.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Next came an angry voice - the Rabbit's - "Pat! Pat! Where are you?" And then a voice she had never heard before, "Sure then I'm here! Digging for apples, yer honour!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Now tell me, Pat, what's that in the window?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "An arm, you goose! Who ever saw one that size? Why, it fills the whole window!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Sure, it does, yer honour: but it's an arm for all that."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, it's got no business there, at any rate: go and take it away!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: There was a long silence after this, and Alice could only hear whispers now and then; such as, "Sure, I don't like it, yer honour, at all, at all!" "Do as I tell you, you coward!" and at last she spread out her hand again, and made another snatch in the air. This time there were two little shrieks, and more sounds of broken glass. "What a number of cucumber-frames there must be!" thought Alice. "I wonder what they'll do next! As for pulling me out of the window, I only wish they could! I'm sure I don't want to stay in here any longer!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh! So Bill's got to come down the chimney, has he?" said Alice to herself. "Shy, they seem to put everything upon Bill! I wouldn't be in Bill's place for a good deal: this fireplace is narrow, to be sure; but I think I can kick a little!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: She drew her foot as far down the chimney as she could, and waited till she heard a little animal (she couldn't guess of what sort it was) scratching and scrambling about in the chimney close above her: then, saying to herself "This is Bill," she gave one sharp kick, and waited to see what would happen next.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The first thing she heard was a general chorus of "There goes Bill!" then the Rabbit's voice along - "Catch him, you by the hedge!" then silence, and then another confusion of voices - "Hold up his head - Brandy now - Don't choke him - How was it, old fellow? What happened to you? Tell us all about it!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Last came a little feeble, squeaking voice, ("That's Bill," thought Alice,) "Well, I hardly know - No more, thank ye; I'm better now - but I'm a deal too flustered to tell you - all I know is, something comes at me like a Jack-in-the-box, and up I goes like a sky-rocket!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "We must burn the house down!" said the Rabbit's voice; and Alice called out as loud as she could, "If you do, I'll set Dinah at you!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: There was a dead silence instantly, and Alice thought to herself, "I wonder what they will do next! If they had any sense, they'd take the roof off." After a minute or two, they began moving about again, and Alice heard the Rabbit say, "A barrowful will do, to begin with."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "A barrowful of what?" thought Alice; but she had not long to doubt, for the next moment a shower of little pebbles came rattling in at the window, and some of them hit her in the face. "I'll put a stop to this," she said to herself, and shouted out, "You'd better not do that again!" which produced another dead silence.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice noticed with some surprise that the pebbles were all turning into little cakes as they lay on the floor, and a bright idea came into her head. "If I eat one of these cakes," she thought, "it's sure to make some change in my size; and as it can't possibly make me larger, it must make me smaller, I suppose."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: So she swallowed one of the cakes, and was delighted to find that she began shrinking directly. As soon as she was small enough to get through the door, she ran out of the house, and found quite a crowd of little animals and birds waiting outside. The poor little Lizard, Bill, was in the middle, being held up by two guinea-pigs, who were giving it something out of a bottle. They all made a rush at Alice the moment she appeared; but she ran off as hard as she could, and soon found herself safe in a thick wood.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "The first thing I've got to do," said Alice to herself, as she wandered about in the wood, "is to grow to my right size again; and the second thing is to find my way into that lovely garden. I think that will be the best plan."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: It sounded an excellent plan, no doubt, and very neatly and simply arranged; the only difficulty was, that she had not the smallest idea how to set about it; and while she was peering about anxiously among the trees, a little sharp bark just over her head made her look up in a great hurry.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: An enormous puppy was looking down at her with large round eyes, and feebly stretching out one paw, trying to touch her. "Poor little thing!" said Alice, in a coaxing tone, and she tried hard to whistle to it; but she was terribly frightened all the time at the thought that it might be hungry, in which case it would be very likely to eat her up in spite of all her coaxing.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This seemed to Alice a good opportunity for making her escape; so she set off at once, and ran till she was quite tired and out of breath, and till the puppy's bark sounded quite faint in the distance.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And yet what a dear little puppy it was!" said Alice, as she leant against a buttercup to rest herself, and fanned herself with one of the leaves: "I should have liked teaching it tricks very much, if - if I'd only been the right size to do it! Oh dear! I'd nearly forgotten that I've got to grow up again! Let me see - how is it to be managed? I suppose I ought to eat or drink something or other; but the great question is, what?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The great question certainly was, what? Alice looked all round her at the flowers and the blades of grass, but she did not see anything that looked like the right thing to eat or drink under the circumstances. There was a large mushroom growing near her, about the same height as herself; and when she had looked under it, and on both sides of it, and behind it, it occurred to her that she might as well look and see what was on the top of it.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: She stretched herself up on tiptoe, and peeped over the edge of the mushroom, and her eyes immediately met those of a large blue caterpillar, that was sitting on the top with its arms folded, quietly smoking a long hookah, and taking not the smallest notice of her or of anything else.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Caterpillar and Alice looked at each other for some time in silence: at last the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth, and addressed her in a languid, sleepy voice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This was not an encouraging opening for a conversation. Alice replied, rather shyly, "I - I hardly know, sir, just at present - at least I know who I was when I got up this morning, but I think I must have been changed several times since then."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "What do you mean by that?" said the Caterpillar sternly. "Explain yourself!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I can't explain myself, I'm afraid, sir," said Alice, "because I'm not myself, you see."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I'm afraid I can't put it more clearly," Alice replied very politely, "for I can't understand it myself to begin with; and being so many different sizes in a day is very confusing."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, perhaps you haven't found it so yet," said Alice; "but when you have to turn into a chrysalis - you will some day, you know - and then after that into a butterfly, I should think you'll feel it a little queer, won't you?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, perhaps your feelings may be different," said Alice; "all I know is, it would feel very queer to me."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You!" said the Caterpillar contemptuously. "Who are you?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Which brought them back again to the beginning of the conversation. Alice felt a little irritated at the Caterpillar's making such very short remarks, and she drew herself up and said, very gravely, "I think, you ought to tell me who you are, first."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Here was another puzzling question; and as Alice could not think of any good reason, and as the Caterpillar seemed to be in a very unpleasant state of mind, she turned away.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Come back!" the Caterpillar called after her. "I've something important to say!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This sounded promising, certainly: Alice turned and came back again.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Is that all?" said Alice, swallowing down her anger as well as she could.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice thought she might as well wait, as she had nothing else to do, and perhaps after all it might tell her something worth hearing. For some minutes it puffed away without speaking, but at last it unfolded its arms, took the hookah out of its mouth again, and said, "So you think you're changed, do you?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I'm afraid I am, sir," said Alice; "I can't remember things as I used - and I don't keep the same size for ten minutes together!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Can't remember what things?" said the Caterpillar.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, I've tried to say "How doth the little busy bee," but it all came different!" Alice replied in a very melancholy voice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Repeat, 'You are old, Father William,'" said the Caterpillar.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You are old, Father William," the young man said, "And your hair has become very white; And yet you incessantly stand on your head - Do you think, at your age, it is right?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "In my youth," Father William replied to his son, "I feared it might injure the brain; But, now that I'm perfectly sure I have none, Why, I do it again and again."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You are old," said the youth, "as I mentioned before, And have grown most uncommonly fat; Yet you turned a back-somersault in at the door - Pray, what is the reason of that?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "In my youth," said the sage, as he shook his grey locks, "I kept all my limbs very supple By the use of this ointment - one shilling the box - Allow me to sell you a couple?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You are old," said the youth, "and your jaws are too weak For anything tougher than suet; Yet you finished the goose, with the bones and the beak - Pray, how did you manage to do it?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "In my youth," said his father, "I took to the law, And argued each case with my wife; And the muscular strength, which it gave to my jaw, Has lasted the rest of my life."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You are old," said the youth, "one would hardly suppose That your eye was as steady as ever; Yet you balanced an eel on the end of your nose - What made you so awfully clever?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I have answered three questions, and that is enough," Said his father; "don't give yourself airs! Do you think I can listen all day to such stuff? Be off, or I'll kick you down stairs!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "That is not said right," said the Caterpillar.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Not quite right, I'm afraid," said Alice, timidly; "some of the words have got altered."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It is wrong from beginning to end," said the Caterpillar decidedly, and there was silence for some minutes.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh, I'm not particular as to size," Alice hastily replied; "only one doesn't like changing so often, you know."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice said nothing: she had never been so much contradicted in her life before, and she felt that she was losing her temper.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, I should like to be a little larger, sir, if you wouldn't mind," said Alice: "three inches is such a wretched height to be."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It is a very good height indeed!" said the Caterpillar angrily, rearing itself upright as it spoke (it was exactly three inches high).
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "But I'm not used to it!" pleaded poor Alice in a piteous tone. And she thought of herself, "I wish the creatures wouldn't be so easily offended!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You'll get used to it in time," said the Caterpillar; and it put the hookah into its mouth and began smoking again.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This time Alice waited patiently until it chose to speak again. In a minute or two the Caterpillar took the hookah out of its mouth and yawned once or twice, and shook itself. Then it got down off the mushroom, and crawled away in the grass, merely remarking as it went, "One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "One side of what? The other side of what?" thought Alice to herself.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Of the mushroom," said the Caterpillar, just as if she had asked it aloud; and in another moment it was out of sight.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice remained looking thoughtfully at the mushroom for a minute, trying to make out which were the two sides of it; and as it was perfectly round, she found this a very difficult question. However, at last she stretched her arms round it as far as they would go, and broke off a bit of the edge with each hand.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And now which is which?" she said to herself, and nibbled a little of the right-hand bit to try the effect: the next moment she felt a violent blow underneath her chin: it had struck her foot!
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: She was a good deal frightened by this very sudden change, but she felt that there was no time to be lost, as she was shrinking rapidly; so she set to work at once to eat some of the other bit. Her chin was pressed so closely against her foot, that there was hardly room to open her mouth; but she did it at last, and managed to swallow a morsel of the lefthand bit.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Come, my head's free at last!" said Alice in a tone of delight, which changed into alarm in another moment, when she found that her shoulders were nowhere to be found: all she could see, when she looked down, was an immense length of neck, which seemed to rise like a stalk out of a sea of green leaves that lay far below her.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "What can all that green stuff be?" said Alice. "And where have my shoulders got to? And oh, my poor hands, how is it I can't see you?" She was moving them about as she spoke, but no result seemed to follow, except a little shaking among the distant green leaves.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: As there seemed to be no chance of getting her hands up to her head, she tried to get her head down to them, and was delighted to find that her neck would bend about easily in any direction, like a serpent. She had just succeeded in curving it down into a graceful zigzag, and was going to dive in among the leaves, which she found to be nothing but the tops of the trees under which she had been wandering, when a sharp hiss made her draw back in a hurry: a large pigeon had flown into her face, and was beating her violently with its wings.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I'm not a serpent!" said Alice indignantly. "Let me alone!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Serpent, I say again!" repeated the Pigeon, but in a more subdued tone, and added with a kind of sob, "I've tried every way, and nothing seems to suit them!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I haven't the least idea what you're talking about," said Alice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I've tried the roots of trees, and I've tried banks, and I've tried hedges," the Pigeon went on, without attending to her; "but those serpents! There's no pleasing them!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice was more and more puzzled, but she thought there was no use in saying anything more till the Pigeon had finished.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "As if it wasn't trouble enough hatching the eggs," said the Pigeon; "but I must be on the look-out for serpents night and day! Why, I haven't had a wink of sleep these three weeks!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I'm very sorry you've been annoyed," said Alice, who was beginning to see its meaning.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And just as I'd taken the highest tree in the wood," continued the Pigeon, raising its voice to a shriek, "and just as I was thinking I should be free of them at last, they must needs come wriggling down from the sky! Ugh, Serpent!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well! What are you?" said the Pigeon. "I can see you're trying to invent something!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I - I'm a little girl," said Alice, rather doubtfully, as she remembered the number of changes she had gone through that day.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "A likely story indeed!" said the Pigeon in a tone of the deepest contempt. "I've seen a good many little girls in my time, but never one with such a neck as that! No, no! You're a serpent; and there's no use denying it. I suppose you'll be telling me next that you never tasted an egg!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I have tasted eggs, certainly," said Alice, who was a very truthful child; "but little girls eat eggs quite as much as serpents do, you know."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I don't believe it," said the Pigeon; "but if they do, why then they're a kind of serpent, that's all I can say."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This was such a new idea to Alice, that she was quite silent for a minute or two, which gave the Pigeon the opportunity of adding, "You're looking for eggs, I know that well enough; and what does it matter to me whether you're a little girl or a serpent?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It matters a good deal to me," said Alice hastily; "but I'm not looking for eggs, as it happens; and if I was, I shouldn't want yours: I don't like them raw."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, be off, then!" said the Pigeon in a sulky tone, as it settled down again into its nest. Alice crouched down among the trees as well as she could, for her neck kept getting entangled among the branches, and every now and then she had to stop and untwist it. After a while she remembered that she still held the pieces of mushroom in her hands, and she set to work very carefully, nibbling first at one and then at the other, and growing sometimes taller and sometimes shorter, until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: For a minute or two she stood looking at the house, and wondering what to do next, when suddenly a footman in livery came running out of the wood - (she considered him to be a footman because he was in livery: otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish) - and rapped loudly at the door with his knuckles. It was opened by another footman in livery, with a round face, and large eyes like a frog; and both footmen, Alice noticed, had powdered hair that curled all over their heads. She felt very curious to know what it was all about, and crept a little way out of the wood to listen.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Fish-Footman began by producing from under his arm a great letter, nearly as large as himself, and this he handed over to the other, saying, in a solemn tone, "For the Duchess. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet." The Frog-Footman repeated, in the same solemn tone, only changing the order of the words a little, "From the Queen. An invitation for the Duchess to play croquet."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Then they both bowed low, and their curls got entangled together.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice laughed so much at this, that she had to run back into the wood for fear of their hearing her; and when she next peeped out the Fish-Footman was gone, and the other was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up into the sky.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice went timidly up to the door, and knocked.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "There's no sort of use in knocking," said the Footman, "and that for two reasons. First, because I'm on the same side of the door as you are; secondly, because they're making such a noise inside, no one could possibly hear you." And certainly there was a most extraordinary noise going on within - a constant howling and sneezing, and every now and then a great crash, as if a dish or kettle had been broken to pieces.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Please, then," said Alice, "how am I to get in?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "There might be some sense in your knocking," the Footman went on without attending to her, "if we had the door between us. For instance, if you were inside, you might knock, and I could let you out, you know." He was looking up into the sky all the time he was speaking, and this Alice thought decidedly uncivil. "But perhaps he can't help it," she said to herself; "his eyes are so very nearly at the top of his head. But at any rate he might answer questions. - How am I to get in?" she repeated, aloud.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: At this moment the door of the house opened, and a large plate came skimming out, straight at the Footman's head: it just grazed his nose, and broke to pieces against one of the trees behind him.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "How am I to get in?" asked Alice again, in a louder tone.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Are you to get in at all?" said the Footman. "That's the first question, you know."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: It was, no doubt: only Alice did not like to be told so. "It's really dreadful," she muttered to herself, "the way all the creatures argue. It's enough to drive one crazy!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Footman seemed to think this a good opportunity for repeating his remark, with variations. "I shall sit here," he said, "on and off, for days and days."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Anything you like," said the Footman, and began whistling.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh, there's no use in talking to him," said Alice desperately: "he's perfectly idiotic!" And she opened the door and went in.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The door led right into a large kitchen, which was full of smoke from one end to the other: the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby; the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron which seemed to be full of soup.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "There's certainly too much pepper in that soup!" Alice said to herself, as well as she could for sneezing.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: There was certainly too much of it in the air. Even the Duchess sneezed occasionally; and as for the baby, it was sneezing and howling alternately without a moment's pause. The only things in the kitchen that did not sneeze, were the cook, and a large cat which was sitting on the hearth and grinning from ear to ear.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Please would you tell me," said Alice, a little timidly, for she was not quite sure whether it was good manners for her to speak first, "why your cat grins like that?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It's a Cheshire cat," said the Duchess, "and that's why. Pig!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I didn't know that Cheshire cats always grinned; in fact, I didn't know that cats could grin."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "They all can," said the Duchess; "and most of 'em do."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I don't know of any that do," Alice said very politely, feeling quite pleased to have got into a conversation.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You don't know much," said the Duchess; "and that's a fact."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice did not at all like the tone of this remark, and thought it would be as well to introduce some other subject of conversation. While she was trying to fix on one, the cook took the cauldron of soup off the fire, and at once set to work throwing everything within her reach at the Duchess and the baby - the fire-irons came first; then followed a shower of saucepans, plates, and dishes. The Duchess took no notice of them even when they hit her; and the baby was howling so much already, that it was quite impossible to say whether the blows hurt it or not.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh, please mind what you're doing!" cried Alice, jumping up and down in an agony of terror. "Oh, there goes his precious nose!" as an unusually large saucepan flew close by it, and very nearly carried it off.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "If everybody minded their own business," the Duchess said in a hoarse growl, "the world would go round a deal faster than it does."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Talking of axes," said the Duchess, "chop off her head!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Speak roughly to your little boy, And beat him when he sneezes: He only does it to annoy, Because he knows it teases."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I speak severely to my boy, I beat him when he sneezes; For he can thoroughly enjoy The pepper when he pleases!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Here! you may nurse it a bit, if you like!" the Duchess said to Alice, flinging the baby at her as she spoke. "I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen," and she hurried out of the room. The cook threw a frying-pan after her as she went out, but it just missed her.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice caught the baby with some difficulty, as it was a queer-shaped little creature, and held out its arms and legs in all directions, "just like a star-fish," thought Alice. The poor little thing was snorting like a steam-engine when she caught it, and kept doubling itself up and straightening itself out again, so that altogether, for the first minute or two, it was as much as she could do to hold it.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: As soon as she had made out the proper way of nursing it, (which was to twist it up into a sort of knot, and then keep tight hold of its right ear and left foot, so as to prevent its undoing itself,) she carried it out into the open air. "If I don't take this child away with me," thought Alice, "they're sure to kill it in a day or two: wouldn't it be murder to leave it behind?" She said the last words out loud, and the little thing grunted in reply (it had left off sneezing by this time). "Don't grunt," said Alice; "that's not at all a proper way of expressing yourself."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The baby grunted again, and Alice looked very anxiously into its face to see what was the matter with it. There could be no doubt that it had a very turn-up nose, much more like a snout than a real nose; also its eyes were getting extremely small for a baby: altogether Alice did not like the look of the thing at all. "But perhaps it was only sobbing," she thought, and looked into its eyes again, to see if there were any tears.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: No, there were no tears. "If you're going to turn into a pig, my dear," said Alice, seriously, "I'll have nothing more to do with you. Mind now!" The poor little thing sobbed again (or grunted, it was impossible to say which), and they went on for some while in silence.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice was just beginning to think to herself, "Now, what am I to do with this creature when I get it home?" when it grunted again, so violently, that she looked down into its face in some alarm. This time there could be no mistake about it: it was neither more nor less than a pig, and she felt that it would be quite absurd for her to carry it further.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: So she set the little creature down, and felt quite relieved to see it trot away quietly into the wood. "If it had grown up," she said to herself, "it would have made a dreadfully ugly child: but it makes rather a handsome pig, I think." And she began thinking over other children she knew, who might do very well as pigs, and was just saying to herself, "if one only knew the right way to change them - " when she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards off.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Cat only grinned when it saw Alice. It looked good-natured, she thought: still it had very long claws and a great many teeth, so she felt that it ought to be treated with respect.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Cheshire Puss," she began, rather timidly, as she did not at all know whether it would like the name: however, it only grinned a little wider. "Come, it's pleased so far," thought Alice, and she went on. "Would you tell me, please, which way I ought to go from here?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "That depends a good deal on where you want to get to," said the Cat.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Then it doesn't matter which way you go," said the Cat.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh, you're sure to do that," said the Cat, "if you only walk long enough."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice felt that this could not be denied, so she tried another question. "What sort of people live about here?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "In that direction," the Cat said, waving its right paw round, "lives a Hatter: and in that direction," waving the other paw, "lives a March Hare. Visit either you like: they're both mad."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "But I don't want to go among mad people," Alice remarked.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Oh, you can't help that," said the Cat: "we're all mad here. I'm mad. You're mad."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You must be," said the Cat, "or you wouldn't have come here."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice didn't think that proved it at all; however, she went on "And how do you know that you're mad?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "To begin with," said the Cat, "a dog's not mad. You grant that?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well, then," the Cat went on, "you see, a dog growls when it's angry, and wags its tail when it's pleased. Now I growl when I'm pleased, and wag my tail when I'm angry. Therefore I'm mad."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I call it purring, not growling," said Alice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Call it what you like," said the Cat. "Do you play croquet with the Queen to-day?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I should like it very much," said Alice, "but I haven't been invited yet."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You'll see me there," said the Cat, and vanished.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice was not much surprised at this, she was getting so used to queer things happening. While she was looking at the place where it had been, it suddenly appeared again.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "By-the-bye, what became of the baby?" said the Cat. "I'd nearly forgotten to ask."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It turned into a pig," Alice quietly said, just as if it had come back in a natural way.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I thought it would," said the Cat, and vanished again.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice waited a little, half expecting to see it again, but it did not appear, and after a minute or two she walked on in the direction in which the March Hare was said to live. "I've seen hatters before," she said to herself; "the March Hare will be much the most interesting, and perhaps as this is May it won't be raving mad - at least not so mad as it was in March." As she said this, she looked up, and there was the Cat again, sitting on a branch of a tree.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I said pig," replied Alice; "and I wish you wouldn't keep appearing and vanishing so suddenly: you make one quite giddy."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "All right," said the Cat; and this time it vanished quite slowly, beginning with the end of the tail, and ending with the grin, which remained some time after the rest of it had gone.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Well! I've often seen a cat without a grin," thought Alice; "but a grin without a cat! It's the most curious thing I ever saw in my life!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: She had not gone much farther before she came in sight of the house of the March Hare: she thought it must be the right house, because the chimneys were shaped like ears and the roof was thatched with fur. It was so large a house, that she did not like to go nearer till she had nibbled some more of the lefthand bit of mushroom, and raised herself to about two feet high: even then she walked up towards it rather timidly, saying to herself "Suppose it should be raving mad after all! I almost wish I'd gone to see the Hatter instead!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: There was a table set out under a tree in front of the house, and the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it: a Dormouse was sitting between them, fast asleep, and the other two were using it as a cushion, resting their elbows on it, and talking over its head. "Very uncomfortable for the Dormouse," thought Alice; "only, as it's asleep, I suppose it doesn't mind."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The table was a large one, but the three were all crowded together at one corner of it: "No room! No room!" they cried out when they saw Alice coming. "There's plenty of room!" said Alice indignantly, and she sat down in a large arm-chair at one end of the table.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Have some wine," the March Hare said in an encouraging tone.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice looked all round the table, but there was nothing on it but tea. "I don't see any wine," she remarked.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Then it wasn't very civil of you to offer it," said Alice angrily.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It wasn't very civil of you to sit down without being invited," said the March Hare.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I didn't know it was your table," said Alice; "it's laid for a great many more than three."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Your hair wants cutting," said the Hatter. He had been looking at Alice for some time with great curiosity, and this was his first speech.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You should learn not to make personal remarks," Alice said with some severity; "it's very rude."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Hatter opened his eyes very wide on hearing this; but all he said was, "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Come, we shall have some fun now!" thought Alice. "I'm glad they've begun asking riddles. - I believe I can guess that," she added aloud.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Do you mean that you think you can find out the answer to it?" said the March Hare.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Then you should say what you mean," the March Hare went on.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I do," Alice hastily replied; "at least - at least I mean what I say - that's the same thing, you know."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Not the same thing a bit!" said the Hatter. "You might just as well say that 'I see what I eat' is the same thing as 'I eat what I see'!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You might just as well say," added the March Hare, "that 'I like what I get' is the same thing as 'I get what I like'!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You might just as well say," added the Dormouse, who seemed to be talking in his sleep, "that 'I breathe when I sleep' is the same thing as 'I sleep when I breathe'!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It is the same thing with you," said the Hatter, and here the conversation dropped, and the party sat silent for a minute, while Alice thought over all she could remember about ravens and writing-desks, which wasn't much.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Hatter was the first to break the silence. "What day of the month is it?" he said, turning to Alice: he had taken his watch out of his pocket, and was looking at it uneasily, shaking it every now and then, and holding it to his ear.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice considered a little, and then said "The fourth."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Two days wrong!" sighed the Hatter. "I told you butter wouldn't suit the works!" he added looking angrily at the March Hare.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It was the best butter," the March Hare meekly replied.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Yes, but some crumbs must have got in as well," the Hatter grumbled: "you shouldn't have put it in with the bread-knife."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The March Hare took the watch and looked at it gloomily: then he dipped it into his cup of tea, and looked at it again: but he could think of nothing better to say than his first remark, "It was the best butter, you know."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice had been looking over his shoulder with some curiosity. "What a funny watch!" she remarked. "It tells the day of the month, and doesn't tell what o'clock it is!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Why should it?" muttered the Hatter. "Does your watch tell you what year it is?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Of course not," Alice replied very readily: "but that's because it stays the same year for such a long time together."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Which is just the case with mine," said the Hatter.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice felt dreadfully puzzled, The Hatter's remark seemed to have no sort of meaning in it, and yet it was certainly English. "I don't quite understand you," she said, as politely as she could.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "The Dormouse is asleep again," said the Hatter, and he poured a little hot tea upon its nose.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Dormouse shook its head impatiently, and said, without opening its eyes, "Of course, of course; just what I was going to remark myself."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Have you guessed the riddle yet?" the Hatter said, turning to Alice again.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "No, I give it up," Alice replied: "what's the answer?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I haven't the slightest idea," said the Hatter.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice sighed wearily. "I think you might do something better with the time," she said, "than waste it in asking riddles that have no answers."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "If you knew Time as well as I do," said the Hatter, "you wouldn't talk about wasting it. It's him."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Of course you don't!" the Hatter said, tossing his head contemptuously. "I dare say you never even spoke to Time!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Perhaps not," Alice cautiously replied: "but I know I have to beat time when I learn music."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Ah! that accounts for it," said the Hatter. "He won't stand beating. Now, if you only kept on good terms with him, he'd do almost anything you liked with the clock. For instance, suppose it were nine o'clock in the morning, just time to begin lessons: you'd only have to whisper a hint to Time, and round goes the clock in a twinkling! Half-past one, time for dinner!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "That would be grand, certainly," said Alice thoughtfully: "but then - I shouldn't be hungry for it, you know."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Not at first, perhaps," said the Hatter: "but you could keep it to half-past one as long as you liked."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat! How I wonder what you're at!'
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Here the Dormouse shook itself, and began singing in its sleep "Twinkle, twinkle, twinkle, twinkle - " and went on so long that they had to pinch it to make it stop.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And ever since that," the Hatter went on in a mournful tone, "he won't do a thing I ask! It's always six o'clock now."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: A bright idea came into Alice's head. "Is that the reason so many tea-things are put out here?" she asked.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Yes, that's it," said the Hatter with a sigh: "it's always tea-time, and we've no time to wash the things between whiles."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Then you keep moving round, I suppose?" said Alice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Exactly so," said the Hatter: "as the things get used up."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "But what happens when you come to the beginning again?" Alice ventured to ask.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Suppose we change the subject," the March Hare interrupted, yawning. "I'm getting tired of this. I vote the young lady tells us a story."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I'm afraid I don't know one," said Alice, rather alarmed at the proposal.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Then the Dormouse shall!" they both cried. "Wake up, Dormouse!" And they pinched it on both sides at once.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Dormouse slowly opened his eyes. "I wasn't asleep," he said in a hoarse, feeble voice: "I heard every word you fellows were saying."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And be quick about it," added the Hatter, "or you'll be asleep again before it's done."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "What did they live on?" said Alice, who always took a great interest in questions of eating and drinking.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "They lived on treacle," said the Dormouse, after thinking a minute or two.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "They couldn't have done that, you know," Alice gently remarked; "they'd have been ill."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "So they were," said the Dormouse; "very ill."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice tried to fancy to herself what such an extraordinary way of living would be like, but it puzzled her too much, so she went on: "But why did they live at the bottom of a well?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Take some more tea," the March Hare said to Alice, very earnestly.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I've had nothing yet," Alice replied in an offended tone, "so I can't take more."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You mean you can't take less," said the Hatter: "it's very easy to take more than nothing."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Who's making personal remarks now?" the Hatter asked triumphantly.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice did not quite know what to say to this: so she helped herself to some tea and bread-and-butter, and then turned to the Dormouse, and repeated her question. "Why did they live at the bottom of a well?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Dormouse again took a minute or two to think about it, and then said, "It was a treacle-well."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "There's no such thing!" Alice was beginning very angrily, but the Hatter and the March Hare went "Sh! sh!" and the Dormouse sulkily remarked, "If you can't be civil, you'd better finish the story for yourself."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "No, please go on!" Alice said very humbly; "I won't interrupt again. I dare say there may be one."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "What did they draw?" said Alice, quite forgetting her promise.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Treacle," said the Dormouse, without considering at all this time.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I want a clean cup," interrupted the Hatter: "let's all move one place on."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: He moved on as he spoke, and the Dormouse followed him: the March Hare moved into the Dormouse's place, and Alice rather unwillingly took the place of the March Hare. The Hatter was the only one who got any advantage from the change: and Alice was a good deal worse off than before, as the March Hare had just upset the milk-jug into his plate.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice did not wish to offend the Dormouse again, so she began very cautiously: "But I don't understand. Where did they draw the treacle from?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You can draw water out of a water-well," said the Hatter; "so I should think you could draw treacle out of a treacle-well - eh, stupid?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "But they were in the well," Alice said to the Dormouse, not choosing to notice this last remark.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Of course they were," said the Dormouse; " - well in."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This answer so confused poor Alice, that she let the Dormouse go on for some time without interrupting it.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Dormouse had closed its eyes by this time, and was going off into a doze; but, on being pinched by the Hatter, it woke up again with a little shriek, and went on: " - that begins with an M, such as mouse-traps, and the moon, and memory, and muchness - you know you say things are "much of a muchness" - did you ever see such a thing as a drawing of a muchness?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: This piece of rudeness was more than Alice could bear: she got up in great disgust, and walked off; the Dormouse fell asleep instantly, and neither of the others took the least notice of her going, though she looked back once or twice, half hoping that they would call after her: the last time she saw them, they were trying to put the Dormouse into the teapot.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "At any rate I'll never go there again!" said Alice as she picked her way through the wood. "It's the stupidest tea-party I ever was at in all my life!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Just as she said this, she noticed that one of the trees had a door leading right into it. "That's very curious!" she thought. "But everything's curious today. I think I may as well go in at once." And in she went.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Once more she found herself in the long hall, and close to the little glass table. "Now, I'll manage better this time," she said to herself, and began by taking the little golden key, and unlocking the door that led into the garden. Then she went to work nibbling at the mushroom (she had kept a piece of it in her pocket) till she was about a foot high: then she walked down the little passage: and then - she found herself at last in the beautiful garden, among the bright flower-beds and the cool fountains.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: A large rose-tree stood near the entrance of the garden: the roses growing on it were white, but there were three gardeners at it, busily painting them red. Alice thought this a very curious thing, and she went nearer to watch them, and just as she came up to them she heard one of them say, "Look out now, Five! Don't go splashing paint over me like that!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I couldn't help it," said Five, in a sulky tone; "Seven jogged my elbow."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: On which Seven looked up and said, "That's right, Five! Always lay the blame on others!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You'd better not talk!" said Five. "I heard the Queen say only yesterday you deserved to be beheaded!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "What for?" said the one who had spoken first.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "That's none of your business, Two!" said Seven.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Yes, it is his business!" said Five, "and I'll tell him - it was for bringing the cook tulip-roots instead of onions."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Seven flung down his brush, and had just begun "Well, of all the unjust things - " when his eye chanced to fall upon Alice, as she stood watching them, and he checked himself suddenly: the others looked round also, and all of them bowed low.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Would you tell me," said Alice, a little timidly, "why you are painting those roses?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Five and Seven said nothing, but looked at Two. Two began in a low voice, "Why the fact is, you see, Miss, this here ought to have been a red rose-tree, and we put a white one in by mistake; and if the Queen was to find it out, we should all have our heads cut off, you know. So you see, Miss, we're doing our best, afore she comes, to - " At this moment Five, who had been anxiously looking across the garden, called out "The Queen! The Queen!" and the three gardeners instantly threw themselves flat upon their faces. There was a sound of many footsteps, and Alice looked round, eager to see the Queen.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice was rather doubtful whether she ought not to lie down on her face like the three gardeners, but she could not remember ever having heard of such a rule at processions; "and besides, what would be the use of a procession," thought she, "if people had all to lie down upon their faces, so that they couldn't see it?" So she stood still where she was, and waited.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: When the procession came opposite to Alice, they all stopped and looked at her, and the Queen said severely "Who is this?" She said it to the Knave of Hearts, who only bowed and smiled in reply.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Idiot!" said the Queen, tossing her head impatiently; and, turning to Alice, she went on, "What's your name, child?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "My name is Alice, so please your Majesty," said Alice very politely; but she added, to herself, "Why, they're only a pack of cards, after all. I needn't be afraid of them!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "And who are these?" said the Queen, pointing to the three gardeners who were lying round the rose-tree; for, you see, as they were lying on their faces, and the pattern on their backs was the same as the rest of the pack, she could not tell whether they were gardeners, or soldiers, or courtiers, or three of her own children.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "How should I know?" said Alice, surprised at her own courage. "It's no business of mine."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Nonsense!" said Alice, very loudly and decidedly, and the Queen was silent.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The King laid his hand upon her arm, and timidly said "Consider, my dear: she is only a child!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Queen turned angrily away from him, and said to the Knave "Turn them over!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The Knave did so, very carefully, with one foot.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Get up!" said the Queen, in a shrill, loud voice, and the three gardeners instantly jumped up, and began bowing to the King, the Queen, the royal children, and everybody else.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Leave off that!" screamed the Queen. "You make me giddy." And then, turning to the rose-tree, she went on, "What have you been doing here?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I see!" said the Queen, who had meanwhile been examining the roses. "Off with their heads!" and the procession moved on, three of the soldiers remaining behind to execute the unfortunate gardeners, who ran to Alice for protection.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "You shan't be beheaded!" said Alice, and she put them into a large flower-pot that stood near. The three soldiers wandered about for a minute or two, looking for them, and then quietly marched off after the others.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!" the soldiers shouted in reply.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "That's right!" shouted the Queen. "Can you play croquet?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The soldiers were silent, and looked at Alice, as the question was evidently meant for her.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Come on, then!" roared the Queen, and Alice joined the procession, wondering very much what would happen next.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "It's - it's a very fine day!" said a timid voice at her side. She was walking by the White Rabbit, who was peeping anxiously into her face.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Very," said Alice: " - where's the Duchess?"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Hush! Hush!" said the Rabbit in a low, hurried tone. He looked anxiously over his shoulder as he spoke, and then raised himself upon tiptoe, put his mouth close to her ear, and whispered "She's under sentence of execution."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Did you say 'What a pity!'?" the Rabbit asked.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Get to your places!" shouted the Queen in a voice of thunder, and people began running about in all directions, tumbling up against each other; however, they got settled down in a minute or two, and the game began. Alice thought she had never seen such a curious croquet-ground in her life; it was all ridges and furrows; the balls were live hedgehogs, the mallets live flamingoes, and the soldiers had to double themselves up and to stand on their hands and feet, to make the arches.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: The players all played at once without waiting for turns, quarrelling all the while, and fighting for the hedgehogs; and in a very short time the Queen was in a furious passion, and went stamping about, and shouting "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" about once in a minute.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice began to feel very uneasy: to be sure, she had not as yet had any dispute with the Queen, but she knew that it might happen any minute, "and then," thought she, "what would become of me? They're dreadfully fond of beheading people here; the great wonder is, that there's any one left alive!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: She was looking about for some way of escape, and wondering whether she could get away without being seen, when she noticed a curious appearance in the air: it puzzled her very much at first, but, after watching it a minute or two, she made it out to be a grin, and she said to herself "It's the Cheshire Cat: now I shall have somebody to talk to."
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "How are you getting on?" said the Cat, as soon as there was mouth enough for it to speak with.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: Alice waited till the eyes appeared, and then nodded. "It's no use speaking to it," she thought, "till its ears have come, or at least one of them." In another minute the whole head appeared, and then Alice put down her flamingo, and began an account of the game, feeling very glad she had someone to listen to her. The Cat seemed to think that there was enough of it now in sight, and no more of it appeared.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "I don't think they play at all fairly," Alice began, in rather a complaining tone, "and they all quarrel so dreadfully one can't hear oneself speak - and they don't seem to have any rules in particular; at least, if there are, nobody attends to them - and you've no idea how confusing it is all the things being alive; for instance, there's the arch I've got to go through next walking about at the other end of the ground - and I should have croqueted the Queen's hedgehog just now, only it ran away when it saw mine coming!"
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "How do you like the Queen?" said the Cat in a low voice.
quotes.source: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland — Lewis Carroll

quotes.text: "Not at all," said Alice: "she's so extremely - " Just then she noticed that the Queen was close behind her, listening: so she went on, " - likely to win, that it's hardly worth while finishing the game."
