quotes.text: "They are monstrous beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers," replied the Lion, "and with claws so long and sharp that they could tear me in two as easily as I could kill Toto. I'm terribly afraid of the Kalidahs."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I'm not surprised that you are," returned Dorothy. "They must be dreadful beasts."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Lion was about to reply when suddenly they came to another gulf across the road. But this one was so broad and deep that the Lion knew at once he could not leap across it.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Here is a great tree, standing close to the ditch. If the Tin Woodman can chop it down, so that it will fall to the other side, we can walk across it easily."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That is a first-rate idea," said the Lion. "One would almost suspect you had brains in your head, instead of straw."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Woodman set to work at once, and so sharp was his axe that the tree was soon chopped nearly through. Then the Lion put his strong front legs against the tree and pushed with all his might, and slowly the big tree tipped and fell with a crash across the ditch, with its top branches on the other side.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They had just started to cross this queer bridge when a sharp growl made them all look up, and to their horror they saw running toward them two great beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "They are the Kalidahs!" said the Cowardly Lion, beginning to tremble.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Quick!" cried the Scarecrow. "Let us cross over."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So Dorothy went first, holding Toto in her arms, the Tin Woodman followed, and the Scarecrow came next. The Lion, although he was certainly afraid, turned to face the Kalidahs, and then he gave so loud and terrible a roar that Dorothy screamed and the Scarecrow fell over backward, while even the fierce beasts stopped short and looked at him in surprise.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We are lost, for they will surely tear us to pieces with their sharp claws. But stand close behind me, and I will fight them as long as I am alive."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Wait a minute!" called the Scarecrow. He had been thinking what was best to be done, and now he asked the Woodman to chop away the end of the tree that rested on their side of the ditch. The Tin Woodman began to use his axe at once, and, just as the two Kalidahs were nearly across, the tree fell with a crash into the gulf, carrying the ugly, snarling brutes with it, and both were dashed to pieces on the sharp rocks at the bottom.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Well," said the Cowardly Lion, drawing a long breath of relief, "I see we are going to live a little while longer, and I am glad of it, for it must be a very uncomfortable thing not to be alive. Those creatures frightened me so badly that my heart is beating yet."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Ah," said the Tin Woodman sadly, "I wish I had a heart to beat."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: This adventure made the travelers more anxious than ever to get out of the forest, and they walked so fast that Dorothy became tired, and had to ride on the Lion's back. To their great joy the trees became thinner the farther they advanced, and in the afternoon they suddenly came upon a broad river, flowing swiftly just before them. On the other side of the water they could see the road of yellow brick running through a beautiful country, with green meadows dotted with bright flowers and all the road bordered with trees hanging full of delicious fruits. They were greatly pleased to see this delightful country before them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "How shall we cross the river?" asked Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That is easily done," replied the Scarecrow. "The Tin Woodman must build us a raft, so we can float to the other side."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the Woodman took his axe and began to chop down small trees to make a raft, and while he was busy at this the Scarecrow found on the riverbank a tree full of fine fruit. This pleased Dorothy, who had eaten nothing but nuts all day, and she made a hearty meal of the ripe fruit.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But it takes time to make a raft, even when one is as industrious and untiring as the Tin Woodman, and when night came the work was not done. So they found a cozy place under the trees where they slept well until the morning; and Dorothy dreamed of the Emerald City, and of the good Wizard Oz, who would soon send her back to her own home again.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Our little party of travelers awakened the next morning refreshed and full of hope, and Dorothy breakfasted like a princess off peaches and plums from the trees beside the river. Behind them was the dark forest they had passed safely through, although they had suffered many discouragements; but before them was a lovely, sunny country that seemed to beckon them on to the Emerald City.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: To be sure, the broad river now cut them off from this beautiful land. But the raft was nearly done, and after the Tin Woodman had cut a few more logs and fastened them together with wooden pins, they were ready to start. Dorothy sat down in the middle of the raft and held Toto in her arms. When the Cowardly Lion stepped upon the raft it tipped badly, for he was big and heavy; but the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman stood upon the other end to steady it, and they had long poles in their hands to push the raft through the water.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They got along quite well at first, but when they reached the middle of the river the swift current swept the raft downstream, farther and farther away from the road of yellow brick. And the water grew so deep that the long poles would not touch the bottom.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This is bad," said the Tin Woodman, "for if we cannot get to the land we shall be carried into the country of the Wicked Witch of the West, and she will enchant us and make us her slaves."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And then I should get no brains," said the Scarecrow.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I should get no courage," said the Cowardly Lion.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I should get no heart," said the Tin Woodman.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I should never get back to Kansas," said Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We must certainly get to the Emerald City if we can," the Scarecrow continued, and he pushed so hard on his long pole that it stuck fast in the mud at the bottom of the river. Then, before he could pull it out again - or let go - the raft was swept away, and the poor Scarecrow was left clinging to the pole in the middle of the river.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Good-bye!" he called after them, and they were very sorry to leave him. Indeed, the Tin Woodman began to cry, but fortunately remembered that he might rust, and so dried his tears on Dorothy's apron.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Of course this was a bad thing for the Scarecrow.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am now worse off than when I first met Dorothy," he thought. "Then, I was stuck on a pole in a cornfield, where I could make-believe scare the crows, at any rate. But surely there is no use for a Scarecrow stuck on a pole in the middle of a river. I am afraid I shall never have any brains, after all!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Something must be done to save us. I think I can swim to the shore and pull the raft after me, if you will only hold fast to the tip of my tail."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So he sprang into the water, and the Tin Woodman caught fast hold of his tail. Then the Lion began to swim with all his might toward the shore. It was hard work, although he was so big; but by and by they were drawn out of the current, and then Dorothy took the Tin Woodman's long pole and helped push the raft to the land.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They were all tired out when they reached the shore at last and stepped off upon the pretty green grass, and they also knew that the stream had carried them a long way past the road of yellow brick that led to the Emerald City.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "What shall we do now?" asked the Tin Woodman, as the Lion lay down on the grass to let the sun dry him.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We must get back to the road, in some way," said Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "The best plan will be to walk along the riverbank until we come to the road again," remarked the Lion.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So, when they were rested, Dorothy picked up her basket and they started along the grassy bank, to the road from which the river had carried them. It was a lovely country, with plenty of flowers and fruit trees and sunshine to cheer them, and had they not felt so sorry for the poor Scarecrow, they could have been very happy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They walked along as fast as they could, Dorothy only stopping once to pick a beautiful flower; and after a time the Tin Woodman cried out: "Look!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then they all looked at the river and saw the Scarecrow perched upon his pole in the middle of the water, looking very lonely and sad.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Lion and the Woodman both shook their heads, for they did not know. So they sat down upon the bank and gazed wistfully at the Scarecrow until a Stork flew by, who, upon seeing them, stopped to rest at the water's edge.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Who are you and where are you going?" asked the Stork.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am Dorothy," answered the girl, "and these are my friends, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion; and we are going to the Emerald City."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This isn't the road," said the Stork, as she twisted her long neck and looked sharply at the queer party.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I know it," returned Dorothy, "but we have lost the Scarecrow, and are wondering how we shall get him again."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Over there in the river," answered the little girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If he wasn't so big and heavy I would get him for you," remarked the Stork.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "He isn't heavy a bit," said Dorothy eagerly, "for he is stuffed with straw; and if you will bring him back to us, we shall thank you ever and ever so much."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Well, I'll try," said the Stork, "but if I find he is too heavy to carry I shall have to drop him in the river again."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the big bird flew into the air and over the water till she came to where the Scarecrow was perched upon his pole. Then the Stork with her great claws grabbed the Scarecrow by the arm and carried him up into the air and back to the bank, where Dorothy and the Lion and the Tin Woodman and Toto were sitting.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: When the Scarecrow found himself among his friends again, he was so happy that he hugged them all, even the Lion and Toto; and as they walked along he sang "Tol-de-ri-de-oh!" at every step, he felt so gay.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I was afraid I should have to stay in the river forever," he said, "but the kind Stork saved me, and if I ever get any brains I shall find the Stork again and do her some kindness in return."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That's all right," said the Stork, who was flying along beside them. "I always like to help anyone in trouble. But I must go now, for my babies are waiting in the nest for me. I hope you will find the Emerald City and that Oz will help you."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Thank you," replied Dorothy, and then the kind Stork flew into the air and was soon out of sight.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They walked along listening to the singing of the brightly colored birds and looking at the lovely flowers which now became so thick that the ground was carpeted with them. There were big yellow and white and blue and purple blossoms, besides great clusters of scarlet poppies, which were so brilliant in color they almost dazzled Dorothy's eyes.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Aren't they beautiful?" the girl asked, as she breathed in the spicy scent of the bright flowers.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I suppose so," answered the Scarecrow. "When I have brains, I shall probably like them better."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If I only had a heart, I should love them," added the Tin Woodman.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I always did like flowers," said the Lion. "They seem so helpless and frail. But there are none in the forest so bright as these."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They now came upon more and more of the big scarlet poppies, and fewer and fewer of the other flowers; and soon they found themselves in the midst of a great meadow of poppies. Now it is well known that when there are many of these flowers together their odor is so powerful that anyone who breathes it falls asleep, and if the sleeper is not carried away from the scent of the flowers, he sleeps on and on forever. But Dorothy did not know this, nor could she get away from the bright red flowers that were everywhere about; so presently her eyes grew heavy and she felt she must sit down to rest and to sleep.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But the Tin Woodman would not let her do this.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We must hurry and get back to the road of yellow brick before dark," he said; and the Scarecrow agreed with him. So they kept walking until Dorothy could stand no longer. Her eyes closed in spite of herself and she forgot where she was and fell among the poppies, fast asleep.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If we leave her here she will die," said the Lion. "The smell of the flowers is killing us all. I myself can scarcely keep my eyes open, and the dog is asleep already."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: It was true; Toto had fallen down beside his little mistress. But the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman, not being made of flesh, were not troubled by the scent of the flowers.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Run fast," said the Scarecrow to the Lion, "and get out of this deadly flower bed as soon as you can. We will bring the little girl with us, but if you should fall asleep you are too big to be carried."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the Lion aroused himself and bounded forward as fast as he could go. In a moment he was out of sight.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Let us make a chair with our hands and carry her," said the Scarecrow. So they picked up Toto and put the dog in Dorothy's lap, and then they made a chair with their hands for the seat and their arms for the arms and carried the sleeping girl between them through the flowers.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: On and on they walked, and it seemed that the great carpet of deadly flowers that surrounded them would never end. They followed the bend of the river, and at last came upon their friend the Lion, lying fast asleep among the poppies. The flowers had been too strong for the huge beast and he had given up at last, and fallen only a short distance from the end of the poppy bed, where the sweet grass spread in beautiful green fields before them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We can do nothing for him," said the Tin Woodman, sadly; "for he is much too heavy to lift. We must leave him here to sleep on forever, and perhaps he will dream that he has found courage at last."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I'm sorry," said the Scarecrow. "The Lion was a very good comrade for one so cowardly. But let us go on."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They carried the sleeping girl to a pretty spot beside the river, far enough from the poppy field to prevent her breathing any more of the poison of the flowers, and here they laid her gently on the soft grass and waited for the fresh breeze to waken her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We cannot be far from the road of yellow brick, now," remarked the Scarecrow, as he stood beside the girl, "for we have come nearly as far as the river carried us away."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Tin Woodman was about to reply when he heard a low growl, and turning his head (which worked beautifully on hinges) he saw a strange beast come bounding over the grass toward them. It was, indeed, a great yellow Wildcat, and the Woodman thought it must be chasing something, for its ears were lying close to its head and its mouth was wide open, showing two rows of ugly teeth, while its red eyes glowed like balls of fire. As it came nearer the Tin Woodman saw that running before the beast was a little gray field mouse, and although he had no heart he knew it was wrong for the Wildcat to try to kill such a pretty, harmless creature.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the Woodman raised his axe, and as the Wildcat ran by he gave it a quick blow that cut the beast's head clean off from its body, and it rolled over at his feet in two pieces.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, thank you! Thank you ever so much for saving my life."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Don't speak of it, I beg of you," replied the Woodman. "I have no heart, you know, so I am careful to help all those who may need a friend, even if it happens to be only a mouse."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Only a mouse!" cried the little animal, indignantly. "Why, I am a Queen - the Queen of all the Field Mice!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, indeed," said the Woodman, making a bow.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Therefore you have done a great deed, as well as a brave one, in saving my life," added the Queen.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, your Majesty, we thought you would be killed! How did you manage to escape the great Wildcat?" They all bowed so low to the little Queen that they almost stood upon their heads.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This funny tin man," she answered, "killed the Wildcat and saved my life. So hereafter you must all serve him, and obey his slightest wish."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We will!" cried all the mice, in a shrill chorus. And then they scampered in all directions, for Toto had awakened from his sleep, and seeing all these mice around him he gave one bark of delight and jumped right into the middle of the group. Toto had always loved to chase mice when he lived in Kansas, and he saw no harm in it.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But the Tin Woodman caught the dog in his arms and held him tight, while he called to the mice, "Come back! Come back! Toto shall not hurt you."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: At this the Queen of the Mice stuck her head out from underneath a clump of grass and asked, in a timid voice, "Are you sure he will not bite us?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I will not let him," said the Woodman; "so do not be afraid."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: One by one the mice came creeping back, and Toto did not bark again, although he tried to get out of the Woodman's arms, and would have bitten him had he not known very well he was made of tin. Finally one of the biggest mice spoke.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Is there anything we can do," it asked, "to repay you for saving the life of our Queen?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Nothing that I know of," answered the Woodman; but the Scarecrow, who had been trying to think, but could not because his head was stuffed with straw, said, quickly, "Oh, yes; you can save our friend, the Cowardly Lion, who is asleep in the poppy bed."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "A Lion!" cried the little Queen. "Why, he would eat us all up."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, no," declared the Scarecrow; "this Lion is a coward."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "He says so himself," answered the Scarecrow, "and he would never hurt anyone who is our friend. If you will help us to save him I promise that he shall treat you all with kindness."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Very well," said the Queen, "we trust you. But what shall we do?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Are there many of these mice which call you Queen and are willing to obey you?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Then send for them all to come here as soon as possible, and let each one bring a long piece of string."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Queen turned to the mice that attended her and told them to go at once and get all her people. As soon as they heard her orders they ran away in every direction as fast as possible.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Now," said the Scarecrow to the Tin Woodman, "you must go to those trees by the riverside and make a truck that will carry the Lion."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the Woodman went at once to the trees and began to work; and he soon made a truck out of the limbs of trees, from which he chopped away all the leaves and branches. He fastened it together with wooden pegs and made the four wheels out of short pieces of a big tree trunk. So fast and so well did he work that by the time the mice began to arrive the truck was all ready for them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Permit me to introduce to you her Majesty, the Queen."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy nodded gravely and the Queen made a curtsy, after which she became quite friendly with the little girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Scarecrow and the Woodman now began to fasten the mice to the truck, using the strings they had brought. One end of a string was tied around the neck of each mouse and the other end to the truck. Of course the truck was a thousand times bigger than any of the mice who were to draw it; but when all the mice had been harnessed, they were able to pull it quite easily. Even the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman could sit on it, and were drawn swiftly by their queer little horses to the place where the Lion lay asleep.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: After a great deal of hard work, for the Lion was heavy, they managed to get him up on the truck. Then the Queen hurriedly gave her people the order to start, for she feared if the mice stayed among the poppies too long they also would fall asleep.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: At first the little creatures, many though they were, could hardly stir the heavily loaded truck; but the Woodman and the Scarecrow both pushed from behind, and they got along better. Soon they rolled the Lion out of the poppy bed to the green fields, where he could breathe the sweet, fresh air again, instead of the poisonous scent of the flowers.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy came to meet them and thanked the little mice warmly for saving her companion from death. She had grown so fond of the big Lion she was glad he had been rescued.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then the mice were unharnessed from the truck and scampered away through the grass to their homes. The Queen of the Mice was the last to leave.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If ever you need us again," she said, "come out into the field and call, and we shall hear you and come to your assistance. Good-bye!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Good-bye!" they all answered, and away the Queen ran, while Dorothy held Toto tightly lest he should run after her and frighten her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: After this they sat down beside the Lion until he should awaken; and the Scarecrow brought Dorothy some fruit from a tree near by, which she ate for her dinner.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: It was some time before the Cowardly Lion awakened, for he had lain among the poppies a long while, breathing in their deadly fragrance; but when he did open his eyes and roll off the truck he was very glad to find himself still alive.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I ran as fast as I could," he said, sitting down and yawning, "but the flowers were too strong for me. How did you get me out?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I have always thought myself very big and terrible; yet such little things as flowers came near to killing me, and such small animals as mice have saved my life. How strange it all is! But, comrades, what shall we do now?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We must journey on until we find the road of yellow brick again," said Dorothy, "and then we can keep on to the Emerald City."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So, the Lion being fully refreshed, and feeling quite himself again, they all started upon the journey, greatly enjoying the walk through the soft, fresh grass; and it was not long before they reached the road of yellow brick and turned again toward the Emerald City where the Great Oz dwelt.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This must be the Land of Oz," said Dorothy, "and we are surely getting near the Emerald City."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Yes," answered the Scarecrow. "Everything is green here, while in the country of the Munchkins blue was the favorite color. But the people do not seem to be as friendly as the Munchkins, and I'm afraid we shall be unable to find a place to pass the night."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I should like something to eat besides fruit," said the girl, "and I'm sure Toto is nearly starved. Let us stop at the next house and talk to the people."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So, when they came to a good-sized farmhouse, Dorothy walked boldly up to the door and knocked.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: A woman opened it just far enough to look out, and said, "What do you want, child, and why is that great Lion with you?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We wish to pass the night with you, if you will allow us," answered Dorothy; "and the Lion is my friend and comrade, and would not hurt you for the world."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Is he tame?" asked the woman, opening the door a little wider.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, yes," said the girl, "and he is a great coward, too. He will be more afraid of you than you are of him."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Well," said the woman, after thinking it over and taking another peep at the Lion, "if that is the case you may come in, and I will give you some supper and a place to sleep."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "To the Emerald City," said Dorothy, "to see the Great Oz."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, indeed!" exclaimed the man. "Are you sure that Oz will see you?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Why, it is said that he never lets anyone come into his presence. I have been to the Emerald City many times, and it is a beautiful and wonderful place; but I have never been permitted to see the Great Oz, nor do I know of any living person who has seen him."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Never. He sits day after day in the great Throne Room of his Palace, and even those who wait upon him do not see him face to face."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That is hard to tell," said the man thoughtfully. "You see, Oz is a Great Wizard, and can take on any form he wishes. So that some say he looks like a bird; and some say he looks like an elephant; and some say he looks like a cat. To others he appears as a beautiful fairy, or a brownie, or in any other form that pleases him. But who the real Oz is, when he is in his own form, no living person can tell."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That is very strange," said Dorothy, "but we must try, in some way, to see him, or we shall have made our journey for nothing."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Why do you wish to see the terrible Oz?" asked the man.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I want him to give me some brains," said the Scarecrow eagerly.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, Oz could do that easily enough," declared the man. "He has more brains than he needs."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I want him to give me a heart," said the Tin Woodman.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That will not trouble him," continued the man, "for Oz has a large collection of hearts, of all sizes and shapes."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I want him to give me courage," said the Cowardly Lion.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oz keeps a great pot of courage in his Throne Room," said the man, "which he has covered with a golden plate, to keep it from running over. He will be glad to give you some."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I want him to send me back to Kansas," said Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Where is Kansas?" asked the man, with surprise.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I don't know," replied Dorothy sorrowfully, "but it is my home, and I'm sure it's somewhere."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Very likely. Well, Oz can do anything; so I suppose he will find Kansas for you. But first you must get to see him, and that will be a hard task; for the Great Wizard does not like to see anyone, and he usually has his own way. But what do YOU want?" he continued, speaking to Toto. Toto only wagged his tail; for, strange to say, he could not speak.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The woman now called to them that supper was ready, so they gathered around the table and Dorothy ate some delicious porridge and a dish of scrambled eggs and a plate of nice white bread, and enjoyed her meal. The Lion ate some of the porridge, but did not care for it, saying it was made from oats and oats were food for horses, not for lions. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman ate nothing at all. Toto ate a little of everything, and was glad to get a good supper again.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The woman now gave Dorothy a bed to sleep in, and Toto lay down beside her, while the Lion guarded the door of her room so she might not be disturbed. The Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman stood up in a corner and kept quiet all night, although of course they could not sleep.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The next morning, as soon as the sun was up, they started on their way, and soon saw a beautiful green glow in the sky just before them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That must be the Emerald City," said Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: As they walked on, the green glow became brighter and brighter, and it seemed that at last they were nearing the end of their travels. Yet it was afternoon before they came to the great wall that surrounded the City. It was high and thick and of a bright green color.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: In front of them, and at the end of the road of yellow brick, was a big gate, all studded with emeralds that glittered so in the sun that even the painted eyes of the Scarecrow were dazzled by their brilliancy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: There was a bell beside the gate, and Dorothy pushed the button and heard a silvery tinkle sound within. Then the big gate swung slowly open, and they all passed through and found themselves in a high arched room, the walls of which glistened with countless emeralds.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Before them stood a little man about the same size as the Munchkins. He was clothed all in green, from his head to his feet, and even his skin was of a greenish tint. At his side was a large green box.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: When he saw Dorothy and her companions the man asked, "What do you wish in the Emerald City?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We came here to see the Great Oz," said Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The man was so surprised at this answer that he sat down to think it over.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "It has been many years since anyone asked me to see Oz," he said, shaking his head in perplexity. "He is powerful and terrible, and if you come on an idle or foolish errand to bother the wise reflections of the Great Wizard, he might be angry and destroy you all in an instant."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "But it is not a foolish errand, nor an idle one," replied the Scarecrow; "it is important. And we have been told that Oz is a good Wizard."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "So he is," said the green man, "and he rules the Emerald City wisely and well. But to those who are not honest, or who approach him from curiosity, he is most terrible, and few have ever dared ask to see his face. I am the Guardian of the Gates, and since you demand to see the Great Oz I must take you to his Palace. But first you must put on the spectacles."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Because if you did not wear spectacles the brightness and glory of the Emerald City would blind you. Even those who live in the City must wear spectacles night and day. They are all locked on, for Oz so ordered it when the City was first built, and I have the only key that will unlock them."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: He opened the big box, and Dorothy saw that it was filled with spectacles of every size and shape. All of them had green glasses in them. The Guardian of the Gates found a pair that would just fit Dorothy and put them over her eyes. There were two golden bands fastened to them that passed around the back of her head, where they were locked together by a little key that was at the end of a chain the Guardian of the Gates wore around his neck. When they were on, Dorothy could not take them off had she wished, but of course she did not wish to be blinded by the glare of the Emerald City, so she said nothing.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then the green man fitted spectacles for the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman and the Lion, and even on little Toto; and all were locked fast with the key.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then the Guardian of the Gates put on his own glasses and told them he was ready to show them to the Palace. Taking a big golden key from a peg on the wall, he opened another gate, and they all followed him through the portal into the streets of the Emerald City.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Even with eyes protected by the green spectacles, Dorothy and her friends were at first dazzled by the brilliancy of the wonderful City. The streets were lined with beautiful houses all built of green marble and studded everywhere with sparkling emeralds. They walked over a pavement of the same green marble, and where the blocks were joined together were rows of emeralds, set closely, and glittering in the brightness of the sun. The window panes were of green glass; even the sky above the City had a green tint, and the rays of the sun were green.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: There were many people - men, women, and children - walking about, and these were all dressed in green clothes and had greenish skins. They looked at Dorothy and her strangely assorted company with wondering eyes, and the children all ran away and hid behind their mothers when they saw the Lion; but no one spoke to them. Many shops stood in the street, and Dorothy saw that everything in them was green. Green candy and green pop-corn were offered for sale, as well as green shoes, green hats, and green clothes of all sorts. At one place a man was selling green lemonade, and when the children bought it Dorothy could see that they paid for it with green pennies.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: There seemed to be no horses nor animals of any kind; the men carried things around in little green carts, which they pushed before them. Everyone seemed happy and contented and prosperous.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Guardian of the Gates led them through the streets until they came to a big building, exactly in the middle of the City, which was the Palace of Oz, the Great Wizard. There was a soldier before the door, dressed in a green uniform and wearing a long green beard.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Here are strangers," said the Guardian of the Gates to him, "and they demand to see the Great Oz."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Step inside," answered the soldier, "and I will carry your message to him."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Please make yourselves comfortable while I go to the door of the Throne Room and tell Oz you are here."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, no," returned the soldier; "I have never seen him. But I spoke to him as he sat behind his screen and gave him your message. He said he will grant you an audience, if you so desire; but each one of you must enter his presence alone, and he will admit but one each day. Therefore, as you must remain in the Palace for several days, I will have you shown to rooms where you may rest in comfort after your journey."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Thank you," replied the girl; "that is very kind of Oz."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The soldier now blew upon a green whistle, and at once a young girl, dressed in a pretty green silk gown, entered the room. She had lovely green hair and green eyes, and she bowed low before Dorothy as she said, "Follow me and I will show you your room."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: In a wardrobe were many green dresses, made of silk and satin and velvet; and all of them fitted Dorothy exactly.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Make yourself perfectly at home," said the green girl, "and if you wish for anything ring the bell. Oz will send for you tomorrow morning."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The next morning, after breakfast, the green maiden came to fetch Dorothy, and she dressed her in one of the prettiest gowns, made of green brocaded satin. Dorothy put on a green silk apron and tied a green ribbon around Toto's neck, and they started for the Throne Room of the Great Oz.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Are you really going to look upon the face of Oz the Terrible?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Of course," answered the girl, "if he will see me."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, he will see you," said the soldier who had taken her message to the Wizard, "although he does not like to have people ask to see him. Indeed, at first he was angry and said I should send you back where you came from. Then he asked me what you looked like, and when I mentioned your silver shoes he was very much interested. At last I told him about the mark upon your forehead, and he decided he would admit you to his presence."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Just then a bell rang, and the green girl said to Dorothy, "That is the signal. You must go into the Throne Room alone."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: She opened a little door and Dorothy walked boldly through and found herself in a wonderful place. It was a big, round room with a high arched roof, and the walls and ceiling and floor were covered with large emeralds set closely together. In the center of the roof was a great light, as bright as the sun, which made the emeralds sparkle in a wonderful manner.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But what interested Dorothy most was the big throne of green marble that stood in the middle of the room. It was shaped like a chair and sparkled with gems, as did everything else. In the center of the chair was an enormous Head, without a body to support it or any arms or legs whatever. There was no hair upon this head, but it had eyes and a nose and mouth, and was much bigger than the head of the biggest giant.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am Oz, the Great and Terrible. Who are you, and why do you seek me?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am Dorothy, the Small and Meek. I have come to you for help."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I got them from the Wicked Witch of the East, when my house fell on her and killed her," she replied.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Where did you get the mark upon your forehead?" continued the voice.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That is where the Good Witch of the North kissed me when she bade me good-bye and sent me to you," said the girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Again the eyes looked at her sharply, and they saw she was telling the truth. Then Oz asked, "What do you wish me to do?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Send me back to Kansas, where my Aunt Em and Uncle Henry are," she answered earnestly. "I don't like your country, although it is so beautiful. And I am sure Aunt Em will be dreadfully worried over my being away so long."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The eyes winked three times, and then they turned up to the ceiling and down to the floor and rolled around so queerly that they seemed to see every part of the room. And at last they looked at Dorothy again.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Because you are strong and I am weak; because you are a Great Wizard and I am only a little girl."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "But you were strong enough to kill the Wicked Witch of the East," said Oz.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That just happened," returned Dorothy simply; "I could not help it."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Well," said the Head, "I will give you my answer. You have no right to expect me to send you back to Kansas unless you do something for me in return. In this country everyone must pay for everything he gets. If you wish me to use my magic power to send you home again you must do something for me first. Help me and I will help you."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Kill the Wicked Witch of the West," answered Oz.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "But I cannot!" exclaimed Dorothy, greatly surprised.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "You killed the Witch of the East and you wear the silver shoes, which bear a powerful charm. There is now but one Wicked Witch left in all this land, and when you can tell me she is dead I will send you back to Kansas - but not before."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The little girl began to weep, she was so much disappointed; and the eyes winked again and looked upon her anxiously, as if the Great Oz felt that she could help him if she would.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I never killed anything, willingly," she sobbed. "Even if I wanted to, how could I kill the Wicked Witch? If you, who are Great and Terrible, cannot kill her yourself, how do you expect me to do it?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I do not know," said the Head; "but that is my answer, and until the Wicked Witch dies you will not see your uncle and aunt again. Remember that the Witch is Wicked - tremendously Wicked - and ought to be killed. Now go, and do not ask to see me again until you have done your task."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Sorrowfully Dorothy left the Throne Room and went back where the Lion and the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman were waiting to hear what Oz had said to her. "There is no hope for me," she said sadly, "for Oz will not send me home until I have killed the Wicked Witch of the West; and that I can never do."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Her friends were sorry, but could do nothing to help her; so Dorothy went to her own room and lay down on the bed and cried herself to sleep.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the Scarecrow followed him and was admitted into the great Throne Room, where he saw, sitting in the emerald throne, a most lovely Lady. She was dressed in green silk gauze and wore upon her flowing green locks a crown of jewels. Growing from her shoulders were wings, gorgeous in color and so light that they fluttered if the slightest breath of air reached them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Now the Scarecrow, who had expected to see the great Head Dorothy had told him of, was much astonished; but he answered her bravely.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am only a Scarecrow, stuffed with straw. Therefore I have no brains, and I come to you praying that you will put brains in my head instead of straw, so that I may become as much a man as any other in your dominions."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Why should I do this for you?" asked the Lady.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Because you are wise and powerful, and no one else can help me," answered the Scarecrow.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I never grant favors without some return," said Oz; "but this much I will promise. If you will kill for me the Wicked Witch of the West, I will bestow upon you a great many brains, and such good brains that you will be the wisest man in all the Land of Oz."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I thought you asked Dorothy to kill the Witch," said the Scarecrow, in surprise.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "So I did. I don't care who kills her. But until she is dead I will not grant your wish. Now go, and do not seek me again until you have earned the brains you so greatly desire."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Scarecrow went sorrowfully back to his friends and told them what Oz had said; and Dorothy was surprised to find that the Great Wizard was not a Head, as she had seen him, but a lovely Lady.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "All the same," said the Scarecrow, "she needs a heart as much as the Tin Woodman."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So the Tin Woodman followed him and came to the great Throne Room. He did not know whether he would find Oz a lovely Lady or a Head, but he hoped it would be the lovely Lady. "For," he said to himself, "if it is the head, I am sure I shall not be given a heart, since a head has no heart of its own and therefore cannot feel for me. But if it is the lovely Lady I shall beg hard for a heart, for all ladies are themselves said to be kindly hearted."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am Oz, the Great and Terrible," spoke the Beast, in a voice that was one great roar. "Who are you, and why do you seek me?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I am a Woodman, and made of tin. Therefore I have no heart, and cannot love. I pray you to give me a heart that I may be as other men are."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Because I ask it, and you alone can grant my request," answered the Woodman.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Oz gave a low growl at this, but said, gruffly: "If you indeed desire a heart, you must earn it."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Help Dorothy to kill the Wicked Witch of the West," replied the Beast. "When the Witch is dead, come to me, and I will then give you the biggest and kindest and most loving heart in all the Land of Oz."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If he is a Beast when I go to see him, I shall roar my loudest, and so frighten him that he will grant all I ask. And if he is the lovely Lady, I shall pretend to spring upon her, and so compel her to do my bidding. And if he is the great Head, he will be at my mercy; for I will roll this head all about the room until he promises to give us what we desire. So be of good cheer, my friends, for all will yet be well."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The next morning the soldier with the green whiskers led the Lion to the great Throne Room and bade him enter the presence of Oz.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Lion at once passed through the door, and glancing around saw, to his surprise, that before the throne was a Ball of Fire, so fierce and glowing he could scarcely bear to gaze upon it. His first thought was that Oz had by accident caught on fire and was burning up; but when he tried to go nearer, the heat was so intense that it singed his whiskers, and he crept back tremblingly to a spot nearer the door.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: And the Lion answered, "I am a Cowardly Lion, afraid of everything. I came to you to beg that you give me courage, so that in reality I may become the King of Beasts, as men call me."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Why should I give you courage?" demanded Oz.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Because of all Wizards you are the greatest, and alone have power to grant my request," answered the Lion.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Ball of Fire burned fiercely for a time, and the voice said, "Bring me proof that the Wicked Witch is dead, and that moment I will give you courage. But as long as the Witch lives, you must remain a coward."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Lion was angry at this speech, but could say nothing in reply, and while he stood silently gazing at the Ball of Fire it became so furiously hot that he turned tail and rushed from the room. He was glad to find his friends waiting for him, and told them of his terrible interview with the Wizard.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "There is only one thing we can do," returned the Lion, "and that is to go to the land of the Winkies, seek out the Wicked Witch, and destroy her."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Then I shall never have courage," declared the Lion.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I shall never have brains," added the Scarecrow.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I shall never have a heart," spoke the Tin Woodman.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I shall never see Aunt Em and Uncle Henry," said Dorothy, beginning to cry.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Be careful!" cried the green girl. "The tears will fall on your green silk gown and spot it."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So Dorothy dried her eyes and said, "I suppose we must try it; but I am sure I do not want to kill anybody, even to see Aunt Em again."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I will go with you; but I'm too much of a coward to kill the Witch," said the Lion.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I will go too," declared the Scarecrow; "but I shall not be of much help to you, I am such a fool."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I haven't the heart to harm even a Witch," remarked the Tin Woodman; "but if you go I certainly shall go with you."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Therefore it was decided to start upon their journey the next morning, and the Woodman sharpened his axe on a green grindstone and had all his joints properly oiled. The Scarecrow stuffed himself with fresh straw and Dorothy put new paint on his eyes that he might see better. The green girl, who was very kind to them, filled Dorothy's basket with good things to eat, and fastened a little bell around Toto's neck with a green ribbon.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They went to bed quite early and slept soundly until daylight, when they were awakened by the crowing of a green cock that lived in the back yard of the Palace, and the cackling of a hen that had laid a green egg.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The soldier with the green whiskers led them through the streets of the Emerald City until they reached the room where the Guardian of the Gates lived. This officer unlocked their spectacles to put them back in his great box, and then he politely opened the gate for our friends.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Which road leads to the Wicked Witch of the West?" asked Dorothy.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "There is no road," answered the Guardian of the Gates. "No one ever wishes to go that way."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "How, then, are we to find her?" inquired the girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "That will be easy," replied the man, "for when she knows you are in the country of the Winkies she will find you, and make you all her slaves."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Perhaps not," said the Scarecrow, "for we mean to destroy her."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Oh, that is different," said the Guardian of the Gates. "No one has ever destroyed her before, so I naturally thought she would make slaves of you, as she has of the rest. But take care; for she is wicked and fierce, and may not allow you to destroy her. Keep to the West, where the sun sets, and you cannot fail to find her."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They thanked him and bade him good-bye, and turned toward the West, walking over fields of soft grass dotted here and there with daisies and buttercups. Dorothy still wore the pretty silk dress she had put on in the palace, but now, to her surprise, she found it was no longer green, but pure white. The ribbon around Toto's neck had also lost its green color and was as white as Dorothy's dress.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Emerald City was soon left far behind. As they advanced the ground became rougher and hillier, for there were no farms nor houses in this country of the West, and the ground was untilled.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: In the afternoon the sun shone hot in their faces, for there were no trees to offer them shade; so that before night Dorothy and Toto and the Lion were tired, and lay down upon the grass and fell asleep, with the Woodman and the Scarecrow keeping watch.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Now the Wicked Witch of the West had but one eye, yet that was as powerful as a telescope, and could see everywhere. So, as she sat in the door of her castle, she happened to look around and saw Dorothy lying asleep, with her friends all about her. They were a long distance off, but the Wicked Witch was angry to find them in her country; so she blew upon a silver whistle that hung around her neck.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: At once there came running to her from all directions a pack of great wolves. They had long legs and fierce eyes and sharp teeth.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Go to those people," said the Witch, "and tear them to pieces."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Are you not going to make them your slaves?" asked the leader of the wolves.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "No," she answered, "one is of tin, and one of straw; one is a girl and another a Lion. None of them is fit to work, so you may tear them into small pieces."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Very well," said the wolf, and he dashed away at full speed, followed by the others.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: It was lucky the Scarecrow and the Woodman were wide awake and heard the wolves coming.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This is my fight," said the Woodman, "so get behind me and I will meet them as they come."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: He seized his axe, which he had made very sharp, and as the leader of the wolves came on the Tin Woodman swung his arm and chopped the wolf's head from its body, so that it immediately died. As soon as he could raise his axe another wolf came up, and he also fell under the sharp edge of the Tin Woodman's weapon. There were forty wolves, and forty times a wolf was killed, so that at last they all lay dead in a heap before the Woodman.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then he put down his axe and sat beside the Scarecrow, who said, "It was a good fight, friend."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: They waited until Dorothy awoke the next morning. The little girl was quite frightened when she saw the great pile of shaggy wolves, but the Tin Woodman told her all. She thanked him for saving them and sat down to breakfast, after which they started again upon their journey.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Now this same morning the Wicked Witch came to the door of her castle and looked out with her one eye that could see far off. She saw all her wolves lying dead, and the strangers still traveling through her country. This made her angrier than before, and she blew her silver whistle twice.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Straightway a great flock of wild crows came flying toward her, enough to darken the sky.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: And the Wicked Witch said to the King Crow, "Fly at once to the strangers; peck out their eyes and tear them to pieces."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The wild crows flew in one great flock toward Dorothy and her companions. When the little girl saw them coming she was afraid.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But the Scarecrow said, "This is my battle, so lie down beside me and you will not be harmed."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "It is only a stuffed man. I will peck his eyes out."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The King Crow flew at the Scarecrow, who caught it by the head and twisted its neck until it died. And then another crow flew at him, and the Scarecrow twisted its neck also. There were forty crows, and forty times the Scarecrow twisted a neck, until at last all were lying dead beside him. Then he called to his companions to rise, and again they went upon their journey.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: When the Wicked Witch looked out again and saw all her crows lying in a heap, she got into a terrible rage, and blew three times upon her silver whistle.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Forthwith there was heard a great buzzing in the air, and a swarm of black bees came flying toward her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Go to the strangers and sting them to death!" commanded the Witch, and the bees turned and flew rapidly until they came to where Dorothy and her friends were walking. But the Woodman had seen them coming, and the Scarecrow had decided what to do.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Take out my straw and scatter it over the little girl and the dog and the Lion," he said to the Woodman, "and the bees cannot sting them." This the Woodman did, and as Dorothy lay close beside the Lion and held Toto in her arms, the straw covered them entirely.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The bees came and found no one but the Woodman to sting, so they flew at him and broke off all their stings against the tin, without hurting the Woodman at all. And as bees cannot live when their stings are broken that was the end of the black bees, and they lay scattered thick about the Woodman, like little heaps of fine coal.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then Dorothy and the Lion got up, and the girl helped the Tin Woodman put the straw back into the Scarecrow again, until he was as good as ever. So they started upon their journey once more.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Wicked Witch was so angry when she saw her black bees in little heaps like fine coal that she stamped her foot and tore her hair and gnashed her teeth. And then she called a dozen of her slaves, who were the Winkies, and gave them sharp spears, telling them to go to the strangers and destroy them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Winkies were not a brave people, but they had to do as they were told. So they marched away until they came near to Dorothy. Then the Lion gave a great roar and sprang towards them, and the poor Winkies were so frightened that they ran back as fast as they could.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: When they returned to the castle the Wicked Witch beat them well with a strap, and sent them back to their work, after which she sat down to think what she should do next. She could not understand how all her plans to destroy these strangers had failed; but she was a powerful Witch, as well as a wicked one, and she soon made up her mind how to act.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Now the charm began to work. The sky was darkened, and a low rumbling sound was heard in the air. There was a rushing of many wings, a great chattering and laughing, and the sun came out of the dark sky to show the Wicked Witch surrounded by a crowd of monkeys, each with a pair of immense and powerful wings on his shoulders.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: One, much bigger than the others, seemed to be their leader. He flew close to the Witch and said, "You have called us for the third and last time. What do you command?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Go to the strangers who are within my land and destroy them all except the Lion," said the Wicked Witch. "Bring that beast to me, for I have a mind to harness him like a horse, and make him work."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Your commands shall be obeyed," said the leader. Then, with a great deal of chattering and noise, the Winged Monkeys flew away to the place where Dorothy and her friends were walking.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Some of the Monkeys seized the Tin Woodman and carried him through the air until they were over a country thickly covered with sharp rocks. Here they dropped the poor Woodman, who fell a great distance to the rocks, where he lay so battered and dented that he could neither move nor groan.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Others of the Monkeys caught the Scarecrow, and with their long fingers pulled all of the straw out of his clothes and head. They made his hat and boots and clothes into a small bundle and threw it into the top branches of a tall tree.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The remaining Monkeys threw pieces of stout rope around the Lion and wound many coils about his body and head and legs, until he was unable to bite or scratch or struggle in any way. Then they lifted him up and flew away with him to the Witch's castle, where he was placed in a small yard with a high iron fence around it, so that he could not escape.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But Dorothy they did not harm at all. She stood, with Toto in her arms, watching the sad fate of her comrades and thinking it would soon be her turn. The leader of the Winged Monkeys flew up to her, his long, hairy arms stretched out and his ugly face grinning terribly; but he saw the mark of the Good Witch's kiss upon her forehead and stopped short, motioning the others not to touch her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We dare not harm this little girl," he said to them, "for she is protected by the Power of Good, and that is greater than the Power of Evil. All we can do is to carry her to the castle of the Wicked Witch and leave her there."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "We have obeyed you as far as we were able. The Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow are destroyed, and the Lion is tied up in your yard. The little girl we dare not harm, nor the dog she carries in her arms. Your power over our band is now ended, and you will never see us again."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then all the Winged Monkeys, with much laughing and chattering and noise, flew into the air and were soon out of sight.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Come with me; and see that you mind everything I tell you, for if you do not I will make an end of you, as I did of the Tin Woodman and the Scarecrow."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy followed her through many of the beautiful rooms in her castle until they came to the kitchen, where the Witch bade her clean the pots and kettles and sweep the floor and keep the fire fed with wood.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy went to work meekly, with her mind made up to work as hard as she could; for she was glad the Wicked Witch had decided not to kill her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: With Dorothy hard at work, the Witch thought she would go into the courtyard and harness the Cowardly Lion like a horse; it would amuse her, she was sure, to make him draw her chariot whenever she wished to go to drive. But as she opened the gate the Lion gave a loud roar and bounded at her so fiercely that the Witch was afraid, and ran out and shut the gate again.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If I cannot harness you," said the Witch to the Lion, speaking through the bars of the gate, "I can starve you. You shall have nothing to eat until you do as I wish."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: So after that she took no food to the imprisoned Lion; but every day she came to the gate at noon and asked, "Are you ready to be harnessed like a horse?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: And the Lion would answer, "No. If you come in this yard, I will bite you."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The reason the Lion did not have to do as the Witch wished was that every night, while the woman was asleep, Dorothy carried him food from the cupboard. After he had eaten he would lie down on his bed of straw, and Dorothy would lie beside him and put her head on his soft, shaggy mane, while they talked of their troubles and tried to plan some way to escape. But they could find no way to get out of the castle, for it was constantly guarded by the yellow Winkies, who were the slaves of the Wicked Witch and too afraid of her not to do as she told them.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The girl had to work hard during the day, and often the Witch threatened to beat her with the same old umbrella she always carried in her hand. But, in truth, she did not dare to strike Dorothy, because of the mark upon her forehead. The child did not know this, and was full of fear for herself and Toto. Once the Witch struck Toto a blow with her umbrella and the brave little dog flew at her and bit her leg in return. The Witch did not bleed where she was bitten, for she was so wicked that the blood in her had dried up many years before.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy's life became very sad as she grew to understand that it would be harder than ever to get back to Kansas and Aunt Em again. Sometimes she would cry bitterly for hours, with Toto sitting at her feet and looking into her face, whining dismally to show how sorry he was for his little mistress. Toto did not really care whether he was in Kansas or the Land of Oz so long as Dorothy was with him; but he knew the little girl was unhappy, and that made him unhappy too.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: But the wicked creature was very cunning, and she finally thought of a trick that would give her what she wanted. She placed a bar of iron in the middle of the kitchen floor, and then by her magic arts made the iron invisible to human eyes. So that when Dorothy walked across the floor she stumbled over the bar, not being able to see it, and fell at full length. She was not much hurt, but in her fall one of the Silver Shoes came off; and before she could reach it, the Witch had snatched it away and put it on her own skinny foot.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The wicked woman was greatly pleased with the success of her trick, for as long as she had one of the shoes she owned half the power of their charm, and Dorothy could not use it against her, even had she known how to do so.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The little girl, seeing she had lost one of her pretty shoes, grew angry, and said to the Witch, "Give me back my shoe!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I will not," retorted the Witch, "for it is now my shoe, and not yours."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "You are a wicked creature!" cried Dorothy. "You have no right to take my shoe from me."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I shall keep it, just the same," said the Witch, laughing at her, "and someday I shall get the other one from you, too."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: This made Dorothy so very angry that she picked up the bucket of water that stood near and dashed it over the Witch, wetting her from head to foot.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Instantly the wicked woman gave a loud cry of fear, and then, as Dorothy looked at her in wonder, the Witch began to shrink and fall away.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "See what you have done!" she screamed. "In a minute I shall melt away."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I'm very sorry, indeed," said Dorothy, who was truly frightened to see the Witch actually melting away like brown sugar before her very eyes.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Didn't you know water would be the end of me?" asked the Witch, in a wailing, despairing voice.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Of course not," answered Dorothy. "How should I?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Well, in a few minutes I shall be all melted, and you will have the castle to yourself. I have been wicked in my day, but I never thought a little girl like you would ever be able to melt me and end my wicked deeds. Look out - here I go!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: With these words the Witch fell down in a brown, melted, shapeless mass and began to spread over the clean boards of the kitchen floor. Seeing that she had really melted away to nothing, Dorothy drew another bucket of water and threw it over the mess. She then swept it all out the door. After picking out the silver shoe, which was all that was left of the old woman, she cleaned and dried it with a cloth, and put it on her foot again. Then, being at last free to do as she chose, she ran out to the courtyard to tell the Lion that the Wicked Witch of the West had come to an end, and that they were no longer prisoners in a strange land.
