quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Call the Winged Monkeys," suggested the Tin Woodman. "You have still the right to command them once more."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Very well," she answered, and putting on the Golden Cap she uttered the magic words. The Monkeys were as prompt as ever, and in a few moments the entire band stood before her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "What are your commands?" inquired the King of the Monkeys, bowing low.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Carry us over the hill to the country of the Quadlings," answered the girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "It shall be done," said the King, and at once the Winged Monkeys caught the four travelers and Toto up in their arms and flew away with them. As they passed over the hill the Hammer-Heads yelled with vexation, and shot their heads high in the air, but they could not reach the Winged Monkeys, which carried Dorothy and her comrades safely over the hill and set them down in the beautiful country of the Quadlings.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This is the last time you can summon us," said the leader to Dorothy; "so good-bye and good luck to you."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Good-bye, and thank you very much," returned the girl; and the Monkeys rose into the air and were out of sight in a twinkling.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The country of the Quadlings seemed rich and happy. There was field upon field of ripening grain, with well-paved roads running between, and pretty rippling brooks with strong bridges across them. The fences and houses and bridges were all painted bright red, just as they had been painted yellow in the country of the Winkies and blue in the country of the Munchkins. The Quadlings themselves, who were short and fat and looked chubby and good-natured, were dressed all in red, which showed bright against the green grass and the yellowing grain.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Monkeys had set them down near a farmhouse, and the four travelers walked up to it and knocked at the door. It was opened by the farmer's wife, and when Dorothy asked for something to eat the woman gave them all a good dinner, with three kinds of cake and four kinds of cookies, and a bowl of milk for Toto.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "How far is it to the Castle of Glinda?" asked the child.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "It is not a great way," answered the farmer's wife. "Take the road to the South and you will soon reach it."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "To see the Good Witch who rules here," she answered. "Will you take me to her?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Let me have your name, and I will ask Glinda if she will receive you." They told who they were, and the girl soldier went into the Castle. After a few moments she came back to say that Dorothy and the others were to be admitted at once.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Before they went to see Glinda, however, they were taken to a room of the Castle, where Dorothy washed her face and combed her hair, and the Lion shook the dust out of his mane, and the Scarecrow patted himself into his best shape, and the Woodman polished his tin and oiled his joints.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: When they were all quite presentable they followed the soldier girl into a big room where the Witch Glinda sat upon a throne of rubies.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: She was both beautiful and young to their eyes. Her hair was a rich red in color and fell in flowing ringlets over her shoulders. Her dress was pure white but her eyes were blue, and they looked kindly upon the little girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "What can I do for you, my child?" she asked.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy told the Witch all her story: how the cyclone had brought her to the Land of Oz, how she had found her companions, and of the wonderful adventures they had met with.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "My greatest wish now," she added, "is to get back to Kansas, for Aunt Em will surely think something dreadful has happened to me, and that will make her put on mourning; and unless the crops are better this year than they were last, I am sure Uncle Henry cannot afford it."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Glinda leaned forward and kissed the sweet, upturned face of the loving little girl.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Bless your dear heart," she said, "I am sure I can tell you of a way to get back to Kansas." Then she added, "But, if I do, you must give me the Golden Cap."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Willingly!" exclaimed Dorothy; "indeed, it is of no use to me now, and when you have it you can command the Winged Monkeys three times."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I think I shall need their service just those three times," answered Glinda, smiling.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy then gave her the Golden Cap, and the Witch said to the Scarecrow, "What will you do when Dorothy has left us?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "I will return to the Emerald City," he replied, "for Oz has made me its ruler and the people like me. The only thing that worries me is how to cross the hill of the Hammer-Heads."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "By means of the Golden Cap I shall command the Winged Monkeys to carry you to the gates of the Emerald City," said Glinda, "for it would be a shame to deprive the people of so wonderful a ruler."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Am I really wonderful?" asked the Scarecrow.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Turning to the Tin Woodman, she asked, "What will become of you when Dorothy leaves this country?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: He leaned on his axe and thought a moment. Then he said, "The Winkies were very kind to me, and wanted me to rule over them after the Wicked Witch died. I am fond of the Winkies, and if I could get back again to the Country of the West, I should like nothing better than to rule over them forever."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "My second command to the Winged Monkeys," said Glinda "will be that they carry you safely to the land of the Winkies. Your brain may not be so large to look at as those of the Scarecrow, but you are really brighter than he is - when you are well polished - and I am sure you will rule the Winkies wisely and well."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Then the Witch looked at the big, shaggy Lion and asked, "When Dorothy has returned to her own home, what will become of you?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Over the hill of the Hammer-Heads," he answered, "lies a grand old forest, and all the beasts that live there have made me their King. If I could only get back to this forest, I would pass my life very happily there."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "My third command to the Winged Monkeys," said Glinda, "shall be to carry you to your forest. Then, having used up the powers of the Golden Cap, I shall give it to the King of the Monkeys, that he and his band may thereafter be free for evermore."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "You are certainly as good as you are beautiful! But you have not yet told me how to get back to Kansas."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "Your Silver Shoes will carry you over the desert," replied Glinda. "If you had known their power you could have gone back to your Aunt Em the very first day you came to this country."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "But then I should not have had my wonderful brains!" cried the Scarecrow. "I might have passed my whole life in the farmer's cornfield."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I should not have had my lovely heart," said the Tin Woodman. "I might have stood and rusted in the forest till the end of the world."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "And I should have lived a coward forever," declared the Lion, "and no beast in all the forest would have had a good word to say to me."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "This is all true," said Dorothy, "and I am glad I was of use to these good friends. But now that each of them has had what he most desired, and each is happy in having a kingdom to rule besides, I think I should like to go back to Kansas."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "The Silver Shoes," said the Good Witch, "have wonderful powers. And one of the most curious things about them is that they can carry you to any place in the world in three steps, and each step will be made in the wink of an eye. All you have to do is to knock the heels together three times and command the shoes to carry you wherever you wish to go."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "If that is so," said the child joyfully, "I will ask them to carry me back to Kansas at once."
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: She threw her arms around the Lion's neck and kissed him, patting his big head tenderly. Then she kissed the Tin Woodman, who was weeping in a way most dangerous to his joints. But she hugged the soft, stuffed body of the Scarecrow in her arms instead of kissing his painted face, and found she was crying herself at this sorrowful parting from her loving comrades.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Glinda the Good stepped down from her ruby throne to give the little girl a good-bye kiss, and Dorothy thanked her for all the kindness she had shown to her friends and herself.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Instantly she was whirling through the air, so swiftly that all she could see or feel was the wind whistling past her ears.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: The Silver Shoes took but three steps, and then she stopped so suddenly that she rolled over upon the grass several times before she knew where she was.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: At length, however, she sat up and looked about her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: For she was sitting on the broad Kansas prairie, and just before her was the new farmhouse Uncle Henry built after the cyclone had carried away the old one. Uncle Henry was milking the cows in the barnyard, and Toto had jumped out of her arms and was running toward the barn, barking furiously.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Dorothy stood up and found she was in her stocking-feet. For the Silver Shoes had fallen off in her flight through the air, and were lost forever in the desert.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: Aunt Em had just come out of the house to water the cabbages when she looked up and saw Dorothy running toward her.
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "My darling child!" she cried, folding the little girl in her arms and covering her face with kisses. "Where in the world did you come from?"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: "From the Land of Oz," said Dorothy gravely. "And here is Toto, too. And oh, Aunt Em! I'm so glad to be at home again!"
quotes.source: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum

quotes.text: One frightfully hot morning, when she was about nine years old, she awakened feeling very cross, and she became crosser still when she saw that the servant who stood by her bedside was not her Ayah.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why did you come?" she said to the strange woman. "I will not let you stay. Send my Ayah to me."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The woman looked frightened, but she only stammered that the Ayah could not come and when Mary threw herself into a passion and beat and kicked her, she looked only more frightened and repeated that it was not possible for the Ayah to come to Missie Sahib.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Pig! Pig! Daughter of Pigs!" she said, because to call a native a pig is the worst insult of all.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Is it so very bad? Oh, is it?" Mary heard her say.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Awfully," the young man answered in a trembling voice. "Awfully, Mrs. Lennox. You ought to have gone to the hills two weeks ago."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Oh, I know I ought!" she cried. "I only stayed to go to that silly dinner party. What a fool I was!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: At that very moment such a loud sound of wailing broke out from the servants' quarters that she clutched the young man's arm, and Mary stood shivering from head to foot. The wailing grew wilder and wilder. "What is it? What is it?" Mrs. Lennox gasped.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Someone has died," answered the boy officer. "You did not say it had broken out among your servants."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I did not know!" the Mem Sahib cried. "Come with me! Come with me!" and she turned and ran into the house.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: After that appalling things happened, and the mysteriousness of the morning was explained to Mary. The cholera had broken out in its most fatal form and people were dying like flies. The Ayah had been taken ill in the night, and it was because she had just died that the servants had wailed in the huts. Before the next day three other servants were dead and others had run away in terror. There was panic on every side, and dying people in all the bungalows.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Many things happened during the hours in which she slept so heavily, but she was not disturbed by the wails and the sound of things being carried in and out of the bungalow.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But no one came, and as she lay waiting the house seemed to grow more and more silent. She heard something rustling on the matting and when she looked down she saw a little snake gliding along and watching her with eyes like jewels. She was not frightened, because he was a harmless little thing who would not hurt her and he seemed in a hurry to get out of the room. He slipped under the door as she watched him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How queer and quiet it is," she said. "It sounds as if there were no one in the bungalow but me and the snake."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Almost the next minute she heard footsteps in the compound, and then on the veranda. They were men's footsteps, and the men entered the bungalow and talked in low voices. No one went to meet or speak to them and they seemed to open doors and look into rooms.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What desolation!" she heard one voice say. "That pretty, pretty woman! I suppose the child, too. I heard there was a child, though no one ever saw her."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary was standing in the middle of the nursery when they opened the door a few minutes later. She looked an ugly, cross little thing and was frowning because she was beginning to be hungry and feel disgracefully neglected. The first man who came in was a large officer she had once seen talking to her father. He looked tired and troubled, but when he saw her he was so startled that he almost jumped back.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Barney!" he cried out. "There is a child here! A child alone! In a place like this! Mercy on us, who is she!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I am Mary Lennox," the little girl said, drawing herself up stiffly. She thought the man was very rude to call her father's bungalow "A place like this!" "I fell asleep when everyone had the cholera and I have only just wakened up. Why does nobody come?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It is the child no one ever saw!" exclaimed the man, turning to his companions. "She has actually been forgotten!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why was I forgotten?" Mary said, stamping her foot. "Why does nobody come?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The young man whose name was Barney looked at her very sadly. Mary even thought she saw him wink his eyes as if to wink tears away.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Poor little kid!" he said. "There is nobody left to come."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was in that strange and sudden way that Mary found out that she had neither father nor mother left; that they had died and been carried away in the night, and that the few native servants who had not died also had left the house as quickly as they could get out of it, none of them even remembering that there was a Missie Sahib. That was why the place was so quiet. It was true that there was no one in the bungalow but herself and the little rustling snake.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She knew that she was not going to stay at the English clergyman's house where she was taken at first. She did not want to stay. The English clergyman was poor and he had five children nearly all the same age and they wore shabby clothes and were always quarreling and snatching toys from each other. Mary hated their untidy bungalow and was so disagreeable to them that after the first day or two nobody would play with her. By the second day they had given her a nickname which made her furious.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was Basil who thought of it first. Basil was a little boy with impudent blue eyes and a turned-up nose, and Mary hated him. She was playing by herself under a tree, just as she had been playing the day the cholera broke out. She was making heaps of earth and paths for a garden and Basil came and stood near to watch her. Presently he got rather interested and suddenly made a suggestion.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why don't you put a heap of stones there and pretend it is a rockery?" he said. "There in the middle," and he leaned over her to point.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Go away!" cried Mary. "I don't want boys. Go away!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: For a moment Basil looked angry, and then he began to tease. He was always teasing his sisters. He danced round and round her and made faces and sang and laughed.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Mistress Mary, quite contrary, How does your garden grow? With silver bells, and cockle shells, And marigolds all in a row."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He sang it until the other children heard and laughed, too; and the crosser Mary got, the more they sang "Mistress Mary, quite contrary"; and after that as long as she stayed with them they called her "Mistress Mary Quite Contrary" when they spoke of her to each other, and often when they spoke to her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You are going to be sent home," Basil said to her, "at the end of the week. And we're glad of it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I am glad of it, too," answered Mary. "Where is home?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "She doesn't know where home is!" said Basil, with seven-year-old scorn. "It's England, of course. Our grandmama lives there and our sister Mabel was sent to her last year. You are not going to your grandmama. You have none. You are going to your uncle. His name is Mr. Archibald Craven."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't know anything about him," snapped Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I know you don't," Basil answered. "You don't know anything. Girls never do. I heard father and mother talking about him. He lives in a great, big, desolate old house in the country and no one goes near him. He's so cross he won't let them, and they wouldn't come if he would let them. He's a hunchback, and he's horrid."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't believe you," said Mary; and she turned her back and stuck her fingers in her ears, because she would not listen any more.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But she thought over it a great deal afterward; and when Mrs. Crawford told her that night that she was going to sail away to England in a few days and go to her uncle, Mr. Archibald Craven, who lived at Misselthwaite Manor, she looked so stony and stubbornly uninterested that they did not know what to think about her. They tried to be kind to her, but she only turned her face away when Mrs. Crawford attempted to kiss her, and held herself stiffly when Mr. Crawford patted her shoulder.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "She is such a plain child," Mrs. Crawford said pityingly, afterward. "And her mother was such a pretty creature. She had a very pretty manner, too, and Mary has the most unattractive ways I ever saw in a child. The children call her 'Mistress Mary Quite Contrary,' and though it's naughty of them, one can't help understanding it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Perhaps if her mother had carried her pretty face and her pretty manners oftener into the nursery Mary might have learned some pretty ways too. It is very sad, now the poor beautiful thing is gone, to remember that many people never even knew that she had a child at all."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I believe she scarcely ever looked at her," sighed Mrs. Crawford. "When her Ayah was dead there was no one to give a thought to the little thing. Think of the servants running away and leaving her all alone in that deserted bungalow. Colonel McGrew said he nearly jumped out of his skin when he opened the door and found her standing by herself in the middle of the room."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "My word! she's a plain little piece of goods!" she said. "And we'd heard that her mother was a beauty. She hasn't handed much of it down, has she, ma'am?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Perhaps she will improve as she grows older," the officer's wife said good-naturedly. "If she were not so sallow and had a nicer expression, her features are rather good. Children alter so much."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "She'll have to alter a good deal," answered Mrs. Medlock. "And, there's nothing likely to improve children at Misselthwaite - if you ask me!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: They thought Mary was not listening because she was standing a little apart from them at the window of the private hotel they had gone to. She was watching the passing buses and cabs and people, but she heard quite well and was made very curious about her uncle and the place he lived in. What sort of a place was it, and what would he be like? What was a hunchback? She had never seen one. Perhaps there were none in India.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Since she had been living in other people's houses and had had no Ayah, she had begun to feel lonely and to think queer thoughts which were new to her. She had begun to wonder why she had never seemed to belong to anyone even when her father and mother had been alive. Other children seemed to belong to their fathers and mothers, but she had never seemed to really be anyone's little girl. She had had servants, and food and clothes, but no one had taken any notice of her. She did not know that this was because she was a disagreeable child; but then, of course, she did not know she was disagreeable. She often thought that other people were, but she did not know that she was so herself.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She thought Mrs. Medlock the most disagreeable person she had ever seen, with her common, highly colored face and her common fine bonnet. When the next day they set out on their journey to Yorkshire, she walked through the station to the railway carriage with her head up and trying to keep as far away from her as she could, because she did not want to seem to belong to her. It would have made her angry to think people imagined she was her little girl.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But Mrs. Medlock was not in the least disturbed by her and her thoughts. She was the kind of woman who would "stand no nonsense from young ones." At least, that is what she would have said if she had been asked. She had not wanted to go to London just when her sister Maria's daughter was going to be married, but she had a comfortable, well paid place as housekeeper at Misselthwaite Manor and the only way in which she could keep it was to do at once what Mr. Archibald Craven told her to do. She never dared even to ask a question.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Captain Lennox and his wife died of the cholera," Mr. Craven had said in his short, cold way. "Captain Lennox was my wife's brother and I am their daughter's guardian. The child is to be brought here. You must go to London and bring her yourself."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: So she packed her small trunk and made the journey.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "A more marred-looking young one I never saw in my life," Mrs. Medlock thought. (Marred is a Yorkshire word and means spoiled and pettish.) She had never seen a child who sat so still without doing anything; and at last she got tired of watching her and began to talk in a brisk, hard voice.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I suppose I may as well tell you something about where you are going to," she said. "Do you know anything about your uncle?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Never heard your father and mother talk about him?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No," said Mary frowning. She frowned because she remembered that her father and mother had never talked to her about anything in particular. Certainly they had never told her things.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Humph," muttered Mrs. Medlock, staring at her queer, unresponsive little face. She did not say any more for a few moments and then she began again.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I suppose you might as well be told something - to prepare you. You are going to a queer place."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary said nothing at all, and Mrs. Medlock looked rather discomfited by her apparent indifference, but, after taking a breath, she went on.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Not but that it's a grand big place in a gloomy way, and Mr. Craven's proud of it in his way - and that's gloomy enough, too. The house is six hundred years old and it's on the edge of the moor, and there's near a hundred rooms in it, though most of them's shut up and locked. And there's pictures and fine old furniture and things that's been there for ages, and there's a big park round it and gardens and trees with branches trailing to the ground - some of them." She paused and took another breath. "But there's nothing else," she ended suddenly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary had begun to listen in spite of herself. It all sounded so unlike India, and anything new rather attracted her. But she did not intend to look as if she were interested. That was one of her unhappy, disagreeable ways. So she sat still.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well," said Mrs. Medlock. "What do you think of it?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Nothing," she answered. "I know nothing about such places."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: That made Mrs. Medlock laugh a short sort of laugh.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh!" she said, "but you are like an old woman. Don't you care?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It doesn't matter" said Mary, "whether I care or not."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You are right enough there," said Mrs. Medlock. "It doesn't. What you're to be kept at Misselthwaite Manor for I don't know, unless because it's the easiest way. He's not going to trouble himself about you, that's sure and certain. He never troubles himself about no one."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She stopped herself as if she had just remembered something in time.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He's got a crooked back," she said. "That set him wrong. He was a sour young man and got no good of all his money and big place till he was married."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary's eyes turned toward her in spite of her intention not to seem to care. She had never thought of the hunchback's being married and she was a trifle surprised. Mrs. Medlock saw this, and as she was a talkative woman she continued with more interest. This was one way of passing some of the time, at any rate.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Yes, she died," Mrs. Medlock answered. "And it made him queerer than ever. He cares about nobody. He won't see people. Most of the time he goes away, and when he is at Misselthwaite he shuts himself up in the West Wing and won't let anyone but Pitcher see him. Pitcher's an old fellow, but he took care of him when he was a child and he knows his ways."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You needn't expect to see him, because ten to one you won't," said Mrs. Medlock. "And you mustn't expect that there will be people to talk to you. You'll have to play about and look after yourself. You'll be told what rooms you can go into and what rooms you're to keep out of. There's gardens enough. But when you're in the house don't go wandering and poking about. Mr. Craven won't have it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I shall not want to go poking about," said sour little Mary and just as suddenly as she had begun to be rather sorry for Mr. Archibald Craven she began to cease to be sorry and to think he was unpleasant enough to deserve all that had happened to him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And she turned her face toward the streaming panes of the window of the railway carriage and gazed out at the gray rain-storm which looked as if it would go on forever and ever. She watched it so long and steadily that the grayness grew heavier and heavier before her eyes and she fell asleep.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You have had a sleep!" she said. "It's time to open your eyes! We're at Thwaite Station and we've got a long drive before us."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary stood up and tried to keep her eyes open while Mrs. Medlock collected her parcels. The little girl did not offer to help her, because in India native servants always picked up or carried things and it seemed quite proper that other people should wait on one.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The station was a small one and nobody but themselves seemed to be getting out of the train. The station-master spoke to Mrs. Medlock in a rough, good-natured way, pronouncing his words in a queer broad fashion which Mary found out afterward was Yorkshire.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I see tha's got back," he said. "An' tha's browt th' young 'un with thee."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, that's her," answered Mrs. Medlock, speaking with a Yorkshire accent herself and jerking her head over her shoulder toward Mary. "How's thy Missus?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well enow. Th' carriage is waitin' outside for thee."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: A brougham stood on the road before the little outside platform. Mary saw that it was a smart carriage and that it was a smart footman who helped her in. His long waterproof coat and the waterproof covering of his hat were shining and dripping with rain as everything was, the burly station-master included.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: When he shut the door, mounted the box with the coachman, and they drove off, the little girl found herself seated in a comfortably cushioned corner, but she was not inclined to go to sleep again. She sat and looked out of the window, curious to see something of the road over which she was being driven to the queer place Mrs. Medlock had spoken of. She was not at all a timid child and she was not exactly frightened, but she felt that there was no knowing what might happen in a house with a hundred rooms nearly all shut up - a house standing on the edge of a moor.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What is a moor?" she said suddenly to Mrs. Medlock.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Look out of the window in about ten minutes and you'll see," the woman answered. "We've got to drive five miles across Missel Moor before we get to the Manor. You won't see much because it's a dark night, but you can see something."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary asked no more questions but waited in the darkness of her corner, keeping her eyes on the window. The carriage lamps cast rays of light a little distance ahead of them and she caught glimpses of the things they passed. After they had left the station they had driven through a tiny village and she had seen whitewashed cottages and the lights of a public house. Then they had passed a church and a vicarage and a little shop-window or so in a cottage with toys and sweets and odd things set out for sale. Then they were on the highroad and she saw hedges and trees. After that there seemed nothing different for a long time - or at least it seemed a long time to her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: At last the horses began to go more slowly, as if they were climbing up-hill, and presently there seemed to be no more hedges and no more trees. She could see nothing, in fact, but a dense darkness on either side. She leaned forward and pressed her face against the window just as the carriage gave a big jolt.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! We're on the moor now sure enough," said Mrs. Medlock.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The carriage lamps shed a yellow light on a rough-looking road which seemed to be cut through bushes and low-growing things which ended in the great expanse of dark apparently spread out before and around them. A wind was rising and making a singular, wild, low, rushing sound.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's - it's not the sea, is it?" said Mary, looking round at her companion.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No, not it," answered Mrs. Medlock. "Nor it isn't fields nor mountains, it's just miles and miles and miles of wild land that nothing grows on but heather and gorse and broom, and nothing lives on but wild ponies and sheep."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I feel as if it might be the sea, if there were water on it," said Mary. "It sounds like the sea just now."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "That's the wind blowing through the bushes," Mrs. Medlock said. "It's a wild, dreary enough place to my mind, though there's plenty that likes it - particularly when the heather's in bloom."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: On and on they drove through the darkness, and though the rain stopped, the wind rushed by and whistled and made strange sounds. The road went up and down, and several times the carriage passed over a little bridge beneath which water rushed very fast with a great deal of noise. Mary felt as if the drive would never come to an end and that the wide, bleak moor was a wide expanse of black ocean through which she was passing on a strip of dry land.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't like it," she said to herself. "I don't like it," and she pinched her thin lips more tightly together.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The horses were climbing up a hilly piece of road when she first caught sight of a light. Mrs. Medlock saw it as soon as she did and drew a long sigh of relief.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh, I am glad to see that bit o' light twinkling," she exclaimed. "It's the light in the lodge window. We shall get a good cup of tea after a bit, at all events."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was "after a bit," as she said, for when the carriage passed through the park gates there was still two miles of avenue to drive through and the trees (which nearly met overhead) made it seem as if they were driving through a long dark vault.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: They drove out of the vault into a clear space and stopped before an immensely long but low-built house which seemed to ramble round a stone court. At first Mary thought that there were no lights at all in the windows, but as she got out of the carriage she saw that one room in a corner upstairs showed a dull glow.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The entrance door was a huge one made of massive, curiously shaped panels of oak studded with big iron nails and bound with great iron bars. It opened into an enormous hall, which was so dimly lighted that the faces in the portraits on the walls and the figures in the suits of armor made Mary feel that she did not want to look at them. As she stood on the stone floor she looked a very small, odd little black figure, and she felt as small and lost and odd as she looked.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: A neat, thin old man stood near the manservant who opened the door for them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You are to take her to her room," he said in a husky voice. "He doesn't want to see her. He's going to London in the morning."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Very well, Mr. Pitcher," Mrs. Medlock answered. "So long as I know what's expected of me, I can manage."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What's expected of you, Mrs. Medlock," Mr. Pitcher said, "is that you make sure that he's not disturbed and that he doesn't see what he doesn't want to see."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And then Mary Lennox was led up a broad staircase and down a long corridor and up a short flight of steps and through another corridor and another, until a door opened in a wall and she found herself in a room with a fire in it and a supper on a table.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, here you are! This room and the next are where you'll live - and you must keep to them. Don't you forget that!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was in this way Mistress Mary arrived at Misselthwaite Manor and she had perhaps never felt quite so contrary in all her life.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What is that?" she said, pointing out of the window.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha, the young housemaid, who had just risen to her feet, looked and pointed also.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "That's th' moor," with a good-natured grin. "Does tha' like it?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "That's because tha'rt not used to it," Martha said, going back to her hearth. "Tha' thinks it's too big an' bare now. But tha' will like it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, that I do," answered Martha, cheerfully polishing away at the grate. "I just love it. It's none bare. It's covered wi' growin' things as smells sweet. It's fair lovely in spring an' summer when th' gorse an' broom an' heather's in flower. It smells o' honey an' there's such a lot o' fresh air - an' th' sky looks so high an' th' bees an' skylarks makes such a nice noise hummin' an' singin'. Eh! I wouldn't live away from th' moor for anythin'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You are a strange servant," she said from her pillows, rather haughtily.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha sat up on her heels, with her blacking-brush in her hand, and laughed, without seeming the least out of temper.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! I know that," she said. "If there was a grand Missus at Misselthwaite I should never have been even one of th' under housemaids. I might have been let to be scullerymaid but I'd never have been let upstairs. I'm too common an' I talk too much Yorkshire. But this is a funny house for all it's so grand. Seems like there's neither Master nor Mistress except Mr. Pitcher an' Mrs. Medlock. Mr. Craven, he won't be troubled about anythin' when he's here, an' he's nearly always away. Mrs. Medlock gave me th' place out o' kindness. She told me she could never have done it if Misselthwaite had been like other big houses."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Are you going to be my servant?" Mary asked, still in her imperious little Indian way.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I'm Mrs. Medlock's servant," she said stoutly. "An' she's Mr. Craven's - but I'm to do the housemaid's work up here an' wait on you a bit. But you won't need much waitin' on."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha sat up on her heels again and stared. She spoke in broad Yorkshire in her amazement.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What do you mean? I don't understand your language," said Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! I forgot," Martha said. "Mrs. Medlock told me I'd have to be careful or you wouldn't know what I was sayin'. I mean can't you put on your own clothes?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No," answered Mary, quite indignantly. "I never did in my life. My Ayah dressed me, of course."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well," said Martha, evidently not in the least aware that she was impudent, "it's time tha' should learn. Tha' cannot begin younger. It'll do thee good to wait on thysen a bit. My mother always said she couldn't see why grand people's children didn't turn out fair fools - what with nurses an' bein' washed an' dressed an' took out to walk as if they was puppies!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It is different in India," said Mistress Mary disdainfully. She could scarcely stand this.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! I can see it's different," she answered almost sympathetically. "I dare say it's because there's such a lot o' blacks there instead o' respectable white people. When I heard you was comin' from India I thought you was a black too."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What!" she said. "What! You thought I was a native. You - you daughter of a pig!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Who are you callin' names?" she said. "You needn't be so vexed. That's not th' way for a young lady to talk. I've nothin' against th' blacks. When you read about 'em in tracts they're always very religious. You always read as a black's a man an' a brother. I've never seen a black an' I was fair pleased to think I was goin' to see one close. When I come in to light your fire this mornin' I crep' up to your bed an' pulled th' cover back careful to look at you. An' there you was," disappointedly, "no more black than me - for all you're so yeller."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary did not even try to control her rage and humiliation.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You thought I was a native! You dared! You don't know anything about natives! They are not people - they're servants who must salaam to you. You know nothing about India. You know nothing about anything!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She was in such a rage and felt so helpless before the girl's simple stare, and somehow she suddenly felt so horribly lonely and far away from everything she understood and which understood her, that she threw herself face downward on the pillows and burst into passionate sobbing. She sobbed so unrestrainedly that good-natured Yorkshire Martha was a little frightened and quite sorry for her. She went to the bed and bent over her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! you mustn't cry like that there!" she begged. "You mustn't for sure. I didn't know you'd be vexed. I don't know anythin' about anythin' - just like you said. I beg your pardon, Miss. Do stop cryin'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: There was something comforting and really friendly in her queer Yorkshire speech and sturdy way which had a good effect on Mary. She gradually ceased crying and became quiet. Martha looked relieved.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's time for thee to get up now," she said. "Mrs. Medlock said I was to carry tha' breakfast an' tea an' dinner into th' room next to this. It's been made into a nursery for thee. I'll help thee on with thy clothes if tha'll get out o' bed. If th' buttons are at th' back tha' cannot button them up tha'self."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: When Mary at last decided to get up, the clothes Martha took from the wardrobe were not the ones she had worn when she arrived the night before with Mrs. Medlock.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Those are not mine," she said. "Mine are black."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "These are th' ones tha' must put on," Martha answered. "Mr. Craven ordered Mrs. Medlock to get 'em in London. He said 'I won't have a child dressed in black wanderin' about like a lost soul,' he said. 'It'd make the place sadder than it is. Put color on her.' Mother she said she knew what he meant. Mother always knows what a body means. She doesn't hold with black hersel'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The dressing process was one which taught them both something. Martha had "buttoned up" her little sisters and brothers but she had never seen a child who stood still and waited for another person to do things for her as if she had neither hands nor feet of her own.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why doesn't tha' put on tha' own shoes?" she said when Mary quietly held out her foot.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "My Ayah did it," answered Mary, staring. "It was the custom."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She said that very often - "It was the custom." The native servants were always saying it. If one told them to do a thing their ancestors had not done for a thousand years they gazed at one mildly and said, "It is not the custom" and one knew that was the end of the matter.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: If Mary Lennox had been a child who was ready to be amused she would perhaps have laughed at Martha's readiness to talk, but Mary only listened to her coldly and wondered at her freedom of manner. At first she was not at all interested, but gradually, as the girl rattled on in her good-tempered, homely way, Mary began to notice what she was saying.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! you should see 'em all," she said. "There's twelve of us an' my father only gets sixteen shilling a week. I can tell you my mother's put to it to get porridge for 'em all. They tumble about on th' moor an' play there all day an' mother says th' air of th' moor fattens 'em. She says she believes they eat th' grass same as th' wild ponies do. Our Dickon, he's twelve years old and he's got a young pony he calls his own."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He found it on th' moor with its mother when it was a little one an' he began to make friends with it an' give it bits o' bread an' pluck young grass for it. And it got to like him so it follows him about an' it lets him get on its back. Dickon's a kind lad an' animals likes him."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha' doesn't want thy porridge!" Martha exclaimed incredulously.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha' doesn't know how good it is. Put a bit o' treacle on it or a bit o' sugar."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh!" said Martha. "I can't abide to see good victuals go to waste. If our children was at this table they'd clean it bare in five minutes."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why!" echoed Martha. "Because they scarce ever had their stomachs full in their lives. They're as hungry as young hawks an' foxes."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't know what it is to be hungry," said Mary, with the indifference of ignorance.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, it would do thee good to try it. I can see that plain enough," she said outspokenly. "I've no patience with folk as sits an' just stares at good bread an' meat. My word! don't I wish Dickon and Phil an' Jane an' th' rest of 'em had what's here under their pinafores."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why don't you take it to them?" suggested Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's not mine," answered Martha stoutly. "An' this isn't my day out. I get my day out once a month same as th' rest. Then I go home an' clean up for mother an' give her a day's rest."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary drank some tea and ate a little toast and some marmalade.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You wrap up warm an' run out an' play you," said Martha. "It'll do you good and give you some stomach for your meat."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary went to the window. There were gardens and paths and big trees, but everything looked dull and wintry.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Out? Why should I go out on a day like this?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, if tha' doesn't go out tha'lt have to stay in, an' what has tha' got to do?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary glanced about her. There was nothing to do. When Mrs. Medlock had prepared the nursery she had not thought of amusement. Perhaps it would be better to go and see what the gardens were like.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You'll go by yourself," she answered. "You'll have to learn to play like other children does when they haven't got sisters and brothers. Our Dickon goes off on th' moor by himself an' plays for hours. That's how he made friends with th' pony. He's got sheep on th' moor that knows him, an' birds as comes an' eats out of his hand. However little there is to eat, he always saves a bit o' his bread to coax his pets."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was really this mention of Dickon which made Mary decide to go out, though she was not aware of it. There would be, birds outside though there would not be ponies or sheep. They would be different from the birds in India and it might amuse her to look at them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha found her coat and hat for her and a pair of stout little boots and she showed her her way downstairs.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "If tha' goes round that way tha'll come to th' gardens," she said, pointing to a gate in a wall of shrubbery. "There's lots o' flowers in summer-time, but there's nothin' bloomin' now." She seemed to hesitate a second before she added, "One of th' gardens is locked up. No one has been in it for ten years."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why?" asked Mary in spite of herself. Here was another locked door added to the hundred in the strange house.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Mr. Craven had it shut when his wife died so sudden. He won't let no one go inside. It was her garden. He locked th' door an' dug a hole and buried th' key. There's Mrs. Medlock's bell ringing - I must run."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She was just thinking this when she saw that, at the end of the path she was following, there seemed to be a long wall, with ivy growing over it. She was not familiar enough with England to know that she was coming upon the kitchen-gardens where the vegetables and fruit were growing. She went toward the wall and found that there was a green door in the ivy, and that it stood open. This was not the closed garden, evidently, and she could go into it.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She went through the door and found that it was a garden with walls all round it and that it was only one of several walled gardens which seemed to open into one another. She saw another open green door, revealing bushes and pathways between beds containing winter vegetables. Fruit-trees were trained flat against the wall, and over some of the beds there were glass frames. The place was bare and ugly enough, Mary thought, as she stood and stared about her. It might be nicer in summer when things were green, but there was nothing pretty about it now.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Presently an old man with a spade over his shoulder walked through the door leading from the second garden. He looked startled when he saw Mary, and then touched his cap. He had a surly old face, and did not seem at all pleased to see her - but then she was displeased with his garden and wore her "quite contrary" expression, and certainly did not seem at all pleased to see him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What is that?" said Mary, pointing through the other green door.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Another of 'em," shortly. "There's another on t'other side o' th' wall an' there's th' orchard t'other side o' that."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Perhaps it was because she had nothing whatever to do that she thought so much of the deserted garden. She was curious about it and wanted to see what it was like. Why had Mr. Archibald Craven buried the key? If he had liked his wife so much why did he hate her garden? She wondered if she should ever see him, but she knew that if she did she should not like him, and he would not like her, and that she should only stand and stare at him and say nothing, though she should be wanting dreadfully to ask him why he had done such a queer thing.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "People never like me and I never like people," she thought. "And I never can talk as the Crawford children could. They were always talking and laughing and making noises."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She thought of the robin and of the way he seemed to sing his song at her, and as she remembered the tree-top he perched on she stopped rather suddenly on the path.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I believe that tree was in the secret garden - I feel sure it was," she said. "There was a wall round the place and there was no door."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She walked back into the first kitchen-garden she had entered and found the old man digging there. She went and stood beside him and watched him a few moments in her cold little way. He took no notice of her and so at last she spoke to him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I have been into the other gardens," she said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There was nothin' to prevent thee," he answered crustily.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There was no dog at th' door to bite thee," he answered.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There was no door there into the other garden," said Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What garden?" he said in a rough voice, stopping his digging for a moment.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "The one on the other side of the wall," answered Mistress Mary. "There are trees there - I saw the tops of them. A bird with a red breast was sitting on one of them and he sang."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: To her surprise the surly old weather-beaten face actually changed its expression. A slow smile spread over it and the gardener looked quite different. It made her think that it was curious how much nicer a person looked when he smiled. She had not thought of it before.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He turned about to the orchard side of his garden and began to whistle - a low soft whistle. She could not understand how such a surly man could make such a coaxing sound.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Almost the next moment a wonderful thing happened. She heard a soft little rushing flight through the air - and it was the bird with the red breast flying to them, and he actually alighted on the big clod of earth quite near to the gardener's foot.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Here he is," chuckled the old man, and then he spoke to the bird as if he were speaking to a child.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Where has tha' been, tha' cheeky little beggar?" he said. "I've not seen thee before today. Has tha begun tha' courtin' this early in th' season? Tha'rt too forrad."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The bird put his tiny head on one side and looked up at him with his soft bright eye which was like a black dewdrop. He seemed quite familiar and not the least afraid. He hopped about and pecked the earth briskly, looking for seeds and insects. It actually gave Mary a queer feeling in her heart, because he was so pretty and cheerful and seemed so like a person. He had a tiny plump body and a delicate beak, and slender delicate legs.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Will he always come when you call him?" she asked almost in a whisper.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, that he will. I've knowed him ever since he was a fledgling. He come out of th' nest in th' other garden an' when first he flew over th' wall he was too weak to fly back for a few days an' we got friendly. When he went over th' wall again th' rest of th' brood was gone an' he was lonely an' he come back to me."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Doesn't tha' know? He's a robin redbreast an' they're th' friendliest, curiousest birds alive. They're almost as friendly as dogs - if you know how to get on with 'em. Watch him peckin' about there an' lookin' round at us now an' again. He knows we're talkin' about him."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was the queerest thing in the world to see the old fellow. He looked at the plump little scarlet-waistcoated bird as if he were both proud and fond of him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He's a conceited one," he chuckled. "He likes to hear folk talk about him. An' curious - bless me, there never was his like for curiosity an' meddlin'. He's always comin' to see what I'm plantin'. He knows all th' things Mester Craven never troubles hissel' to find out. He's th' head gardener, he is."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The robin hopped about busily pecking the soil and now and then stopped and looked at them a little. Mary thought his black dewdrop eyes gazed at her with great curiosity. It really seemed as if he were finding out all about her. The queer feeling in her heart increased.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Where did the rest of the brood fly to?" she asked.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There's no knowin'. The old ones turn 'em out o' their nest an' make 'em fly an' they're scattered before you know it. This one was a knowin' one an' he knew he was lonely."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mistress Mary went a step nearer to the robin and looked at him very hard.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She had not known before that this was one of the things which made her feel sour and cross. She seemed to find it out when the robin looked at her and she looked at the robin.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The old gardener pushed his cap back on his bald head and stared at her a minute.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Art tha' th' little wench from India?" he asked.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Then no wonder tha'rt lonely. Tha'lt be lonlier before tha's done," he said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He began to dig again, driving his spade deep into the rich black garden soil while the robin hopped about very busily employed.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Ben Weatherstaff," he answered, and then he added with a surly chuckle, "I'm lonely mysel' except when he's with me," and he jerked his thumb toward the robin. "He's th' only friend I've got."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I have no friends at all," said Mary. "I never had. My Ayah didn't like me and I never played with anyone."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It is a Yorkshire habit to say what you think with blunt frankness, and old Ben Weatherstaff was a Yorkshire moor man.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha' an' me are a good bit alike," he said. "We was wove out of th' same cloth. We're neither of us good lookin' an' we're both of us as sour as we look. We've got the same nasty tempers, both of us, I'll warrant."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: This was plain speaking, and Mary Lennox had never heard the truth about herself in her life. Native servants always salaamed and submitted to you, whatever you did. She had never thought much about her looks, but she wondered if she was as unattractive as Ben Weatherstaff and she also wondered if she looked as sour as he had looked before the robin came. She actually began to wonder also if she was "nasty tempered." She felt uncomfortable.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Suddenly a clear rippling little sound broke out near her and she turned round. She was standing a few feet from a young apple-tree and the robin had flown on to one of its branches and had burst out into a scrap of a song. Ben Weatherstaff laughed outright.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He's made up his mind to make friends with thee," replied Ben. "Dang me if he hasn't took a fancy to thee."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "To me?" said Mary, and she moved toward the little tree softly and looked up.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Would you make friends with me?" she said to the robin just as if she was speaking to a person. "Would you?" And she did not say it either in her hard little voice or in her imperious Indian voice, but in a tone so soft and eager and coaxing that Ben Weatherstaff was as surprised as she had been when she heard him whistle.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why," he cried out, "tha' said that as nice an' human as if tha' was a real child instead of a sharp old woman. Tha' said it almost like Dickon talks to his wild things on th' moor."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Do you know Dickon?" Mary asked, turning round rather in a hurry.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Everybody knows him. Dickon's wanderin' about everywhere. Th' very blackberries an' heather-bells knows him. I warrant th' foxes shows him where their cubs lies an' th' skylarks doesn't hide their nests from him."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary would have liked to ask some more questions. She was almost as curious about Dickon as she was about the deserted garden. But just that moment the robin, who had ended his song, gave a little shake of his wings, spread them and flew away. He had made his visit and had other things to do.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He has flown over the wall!" Mary cried out, watching him. "He has flown into the orchard - he has flown across the other wall - into the garden where there is no door!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He lives there," said old Ben. "He came out o' th' egg there. If he's courtin', he's makin' up to some young madam of a robin that lives among th' old rose-trees there."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Rose-trees," said Mary. "Are there rose-trees?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Ben Weatherstaff took up his spade again and began to dig.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I should like to see them," said Mary. "Where is the green door? There must be a door somewhere."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Ben drove his spade deep and looked as uncompanionable as he had looked when she first saw him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There was ten year' ago, but there isn't now," he said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "None as anyone can find, an' none as is anyone's business. Don't you be a meddlesome wench an' poke your nose where it's no cause to go. Here, I must go on with my work. Get you gone an' play you. I've no more time."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And he actually stopped digging, threw his spade over his shoulder and walked off, without even glancing at her or saying good-by.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But after a few days spent almost entirely out of doors she wakened one morning knowing what it was to be hungry, and when she sat down to her breakfast she did not glance disdainfully at her porridge and push it away, but took up her spoon and began to eat it and went on eating it until her bowl was empty.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha' got on well enough with that this mornin', didn't tha'?" said Martha.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It tastes nice today," said Mary, feeling a little surprised herself.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's th' air of th' moor that's givin' thee stomach for tha' victuals," answered Martha. "It's lucky for thee that tha's got victuals as well as appetite. There's been twelve in our cottage as had th' stomach an' nothin' to put in it. You go on playin' you out o' doors every day an' you'll get some flesh on your bones an' you won't be so yeller."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't play," said Mary. "I have nothing to play with."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Nothin' to play with!" exclaimed Martha. "Our children plays with sticks and stones. They just runs about an' shouts an' looks at things." Mary did not shout, but she looked at things. There was nothing else to do. She walked round and round the gardens and wandered about the paths in the park. Sometimes she looked for Ben Weatherstaff, but though several times she saw him at work he was too busy to look at her or was too surly. Once when she was walking toward him he picked up his spade and turned away as if he did it on purpose.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: One place she went to oftener than to any other. It was the long walk outside the gardens with the walls round them. There were bare flower-beds on either side of it and against the walls ivy grew thickly. There was one part of the wall where the creeping dark green leaves were more bushy than elsewhere. It seemed as if for a long time that part had been neglected. The rest of it had been clipped and made to look neat, but at this lower end of the walk it had not been trimmed at all.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: A few days after she had talked to Ben Weatherstaff, Mary stopped to notice this and wondered why it was so. She had just paused and was looking up at a long spray of ivy swinging in the wind when she saw a gleam of scarlet and heard a brilliant chirp, and there, on the top of the wall, perched Ben Weatherstaff's robin redbreast, tilting forward to look at her with his small head on one side.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Oh!" she cried out, "is it you - is it you?" And it did not seem at all queer to her that she spoke to him as if she were sure that he would understand and answer her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Good morning! Isn't the wind nice? Isn't the sun nice? Isn't everything nice? Let us both chirp and hop and twitter. Come on! Come on!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary began to laugh, and as he hopped and took little flights along the wall she ran after him. Poor little thin, sallow, ugly Mary - she actually looked almost pretty for a moment.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I like you! I like you!" she cried out, pattering down the walk; and she chirped and tried to whistle, which last she did not know how to do in the least. But the robin seemed to be quite satisfied and chirped and whistled back at her. At last he spread his wings and made a darting flight to the top of a tree, where he perched and sang loudly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: That reminded Mary of the first time she had seen him. He had been swinging on a tree-top then and she had been standing in the orchard. Now she was on the other side of the orchard and standing in the path outside a wall - much lower down - and there was the same tree inside.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's in the garden no one can go into," she said to herself. "It's the garden without a door. He lives in there. How I wish I could see what it is like!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She ran up the walk to the green door she had entered the first morning. Then she ran down the path through the other door and then into the orchard, and when she stood and looked up there was the tree on the other side of the wall, and there was the robin just finishing his song and beginning to preen his feathers with his beak.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It is the garden," she said. "I am sure it is."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She walked round and looked closely at that side of the orchard wall, but she only found what she had found before - that there was no door in it. Then she ran through the kitchen-gardens again and out into the walk outside the long ivy-covered wall, and she walked to the end of it and looked at it, but there was no door; and then she walked to the other end, looking again, but there was no door.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's very queer," she said. "Ben Weatherstaff said there was no door and there is no door. But there must have been one ten years ago, because Mr. Craven buried the key."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: This gave her so much to think of that she began to be quite interested and feel that she was not sorry that she had come to Misselthwaite Manor. In India she had always felt hot and too languid to care much about anything. The fact was that the fresh wind from the moor had begun to blow the cobwebs out of her young brain and to waken her up a little.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She stayed out of doors nearly all day, and when she sat down to her supper at night she felt hungry and drowsy and comfortable. She did not feel cross when Martha chattered away. She felt as if she rather liked to hear her, and at last she thought she would ask her a question. She asked it after she had finished her supper and had sat down on the hearth-rug before the fire.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Why did Mr. Craven hate the garden?" she said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She had made Martha stay with her and Martha had not objected at all. She was very young, and used to a crowded cottage full of brothers and sisters, and she found it dull in the great servants' hall downstairs where the footman and upper-housemaids made fun of her Yorkshire speech and looked upon her as a common little thing, and sat and whispered among themselves. Martha liked to talk, and the strange child who had lived in India, and been waited upon by "blacks," was novelty enough to attract her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She sat down on the hearth herself without waiting to be asked.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett
