quotes.text: "Art tha' thinkin' about that garden yet?" she said. "I knew tha' would. That was just the way with me when I first heard about it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha tucked her feet under her and made herself quite comfortable.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Listen to th' wind wutherin' round the house," she said. "You could bare stand up on the moor if you was out on it tonight."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary did not know what "wutherin'" meant until she listened, and then she understood. It must mean that hollow shuddering sort of roar which rushed round and round the house as if the giant no one could see were buffeting it and beating at the walls and windows to try to break in. But one knew he could not get in, and somehow it made one feel very safe and warm inside a room with a red coal fire.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "But why did he hate it so?" she asked, after she had listened. She intended to know if Martha did.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary did not ask any more questions. She looked at the red fire and listened to the wind "wutherin'." It seemed to be "wutherin'" louder than ever.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: At that moment a very good thing was happening to her. Four good things had happened to her, in fact, since she came to Misselthwaite Manor. She had felt as if she had understood a robin and that he had understood her; she had run in the wind until her blood had grown warm; she had been healthily hungry for the first time in her life; and she had found out what it was to be sorry for someone.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But as she was listening to the wind she began to listen to something else. She did not know what it was, because at first she could scarcely distinguish it from the wind itself. It was a curious sound - it seemed almost as if a child were crying somewhere. Sometimes the wind sounded rather like a child crying, but presently Mistress Mary felt quite sure this sound was inside the house, not outside it. It was far away, but it was inside. She turned round and looked at Martha.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No," she answered. "It's th' wind. Sometimes it sounds like as if someone was lost on th' moor an' wailin'. It's got all sorts o' sounds."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "But listen," said Mary. "It's in the house - down one of those long corridors."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And at that very moment a door must have been opened somewhere downstairs; for a great rushing draft blew along the passage and the door of the room they sat in was blown open with a crash, and as they both jumped to their feet the light was blown out and the crying sound was swept down the far corridor so that it was to be heard more plainly than ever.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There!" said Mary. "I told you so! It is someone crying - and it isn't a grown-up person."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha ran and shut the door and turned the key, but before she did it they both heard the sound of a door in some far passage shutting with a bang, and then everything was quiet, for even the wind ceased "wutherin'" for a few moments.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It was th' wind," said Martha stubbornly. "An' if it wasn't, it was little Betty Butterworth, th' scullery-maid. She's had th' toothache all day."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But something troubled and awkward in her manner made Mistress Mary stare very hard at her. She did not believe she was speaking the truth.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: CHAPTER VI. "THERE WAS SOMEONE CRYING - THERE WAS!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The next day the rain poured down in torrents again, and when Mary looked out of her window the moor was almost hidden by gray mist and cloud. There could be no going out today.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What do you do in your cottage when it rains like this?" she asked Martha.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The time had come when Mary had forgotten to resent Martha's familiar talk. She had even begun to find it interesting and to be sorry when she stopped or went away. The stories she had been told by her Ayah when she lived in India had been quite unlike those Martha had to tell about the moorland cottage which held fourteen people who lived in four little rooms and never had quite enough to eat. The children seemed to tumble about and amuse themselves like a litter of rough, good-natured collie puppies. Mary was most attracted by the mother and Dickon. When Martha told stories of what "mother" said or did they always sounded comfortable.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "If I had a raven or a fox cub I could play with it," said Mary. "But I have nothing."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Then why doesn't tha read somethin', or learn a bit o' spellin'? Tha'st old enough to be learnin' thy book a good bit now."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I haven't any books," said Mary. "Those I had were left in India."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "That's a pity," said Martha. "If Mrs. Medlock'd let thee go into th' library, there's thousands o' books there."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary did not ask where the library was, because she was suddenly inspired by a new idea. She made up her mind to go and find it herself. She was not troubled about Mrs. Medlock. Mrs. Medlock seemed always to be in her comfortable housekeeper's sitting-room downstairs. In this queer place one scarcely ever saw anyone at all. In fact, there was no one to see but the servants, and when their master was away they lived a luxurious life below stairs, where there was a huge kitchen hung about with shining brass and pewter, and a large servants' hall where there were four or five abundant meals eaten every day, and where a great deal of lively romping went on when Mrs. Medlock was out of the way.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary's meals were served regularly, and Martha waited on her, but no one troubled themselves about her in the least. Mrs. Medlock came and looked at her every day or two, but no one inquired what she did or told her what to do. She supposed that perhaps this was the English way of treating children. In India she had always been attended by her Ayah, who had followed her about and waited on her, hand and foot. She had often been tired of her company. Now she was followed by nobody and was learning to dress herself because Martha looked as though she thought she was silly and stupid when she wanted to have things handed to her and put on.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Hasn't tha' got good sense?" she said once, when Mary had stood waiting for her to put on her gloves for her. "Our Susan Ann is twice as sharp as thee an' she's only four year' old. Sometimes tha' looks fair soft in th' head."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary had worn her contrary scowl for an hour after that, but it made her think several entirely new things.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Where do you live now?" said Mary aloud to her. "I wish you were here."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Surely no other little girl ever spent such a queer morning. It seemed as if there was no one in all the huge rambling house but her own small self, wandering about upstairs and down, through narrow passages and wide ones, where it seemed to her that no one but herself had ever walked. Since so many rooms had been built, people must have lived in them, but it all seemed so empty that she could not quite believe it true.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Perhaps she slept here once," said Mary. "She stares at me so that she makes me feel queer."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: After that she opened more doors and more. She saw so many rooms that she became quite tired and began to think that there must be a hundred, though she had not counted them. In all of them there were old pictures or old tapestries with strange scenes worked on them. There were curious pieces of furniture and curious ornaments in nearly all of them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: In one room, which looked like a lady's sitting-room, the hangings were all embroidered velvet, and in a cabinet were about a hundred little elephants made of ivory. They were of different sizes, and some had their mahouts or palanquins on their backs. Some were much bigger than the others and some were so tiny that they seemed only babies. Mary had seen carved ivory in India and she knew all about elephants. She opened the door of the cabinet and stood on a footstool and played with these for quite a long time. When she got tired she set the elephants in order and shut the door of the cabinet.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: In all her wanderings through the long corridors and the empty rooms, she had seen nothing alive; but in this room she saw something. Just after she had closed the cabinet door she heard a tiny rustling sound. It made her jump and look around at the sofa by the fireplace, from which it seemed to come. In the corner of the sofa there was a cushion, and in the velvet which covered it there was a hole, and out of the hole peeped a tiny head with a pair of frightened eyes in it.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary crept softly across the room to look. The bright eyes belonged to a little gray mouse, and the mouse had eaten a hole into the cushion and made a comfortable nest there. Six baby mice were cuddled up asleep near her. If there was no one else alive in the hundred rooms there were seven mice who did not look lonely at all.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "If they wouldn't be so frightened I would take them back with me," said Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She had wandered about long enough to feel too tired to wander any farther, and she turned back. Two or three times she lost her way by turning down the wrong corridor and was obliged to ramble up and down until she found the right one; but at last she reached her own floor again, though she was some distance from her own room and did not know exactly where she was.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I believe I have taken a wrong turning again," she said, standing still at what seemed the end of a short passage with tapestry on the wall. "I don't know which way to go. How still everything is!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was while she was standing here and just after she had said this that the stillness was broken by a sound. It was another cry, but not quite like the one she had heard last night; it was only a short one, a fretful childish whine muffled by passing through walls.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's nearer than it was," said Mary, her heart beating rather faster. "And it is crying."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She put her hand accidentally upon the tapestry near her, and then sprang back, feeling quite startled. The tapestry was the covering of a door which fell open and showed her that there was another part of the corridor behind it, and Mrs. Medlock was coming up it with her bunch of keys in her hand and a very cross look on her face.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What are you doing here?" she said, and she took Mary by the arm and pulled her away. "What did I tell you?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I turned round the wrong corner," explained Mary. "I didn't know which way to go and I heard someone crying." She quite hated Mrs. Medlock at the moment, but she hated her more the next.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You didn't hear anything of the sort," said the housekeeper. "You come along back to your own nursery or I'll box your ears."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And she took her by the arm and half pushed, half pulled her up one passage and down another until she pushed her in at the door of her own room.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Now," she said, "you stay where you're told to stay or you'll find yourself locked up. The master had better get you a governess, same as he said he would. You're one that needs someone to look sharp after you. I've got enough to do."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She went out of the room and slammed the door after her, and Mary went and sat on the hearth-rug, pale with rage. She did not cry, but ground her teeth.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There was someone crying - there was - there was!" she said to herself.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She had heard it twice now, and sometime she would find out. She had found out a great deal this morning. She felt as if she had been on a long journey, and at any rate she had had something to amuse her all the time, and she had played with the ivory elephants and had seen the gray mouse and its babies in their nest in the velvet cushion.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Two days after this, when Mary opened her eyes she sat upright in bed immediately, and called to Martha.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The rainstorm had ended and the gray mist and clouds had been swept away in the night by the wind. The wind itself had ceased and a brilliant, deep blue sky arched high over the moorland. Never, never had Mary dreamed of a sky so blue. In India skies were hot and blazing; this was of a deep cool blue which almost seemed to sparkle like the waters of some lovely bottomless lake, and here and there, high, high in the arched blueness floated small clouds of snow-white fleece. The far-reaching world of the moor itself looked softly blue instead of gloomy purple-black or awful dreary gray.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye," said Martha with a cheerful grin. "Th' storm's over for a bit. It does like this at this time o' th' year. It goes off in a night like it was pretendin' it had never been here an' never meant to come again. That's because th' springtime's on its way. It's a long way off yet, but it's comin'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I thought perhaps it always rained or looked dark in England," Mary said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! no!" said Martha, sitting up on her heels among her black lead brushes. "Nowt o' th' soart!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What does that mean?" asked Mary seriously. In India the natives spoke different dialects which only a few people understood, so she was not surprised when Martha used words she did not know.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha laughed as she had done the first morning.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There now," she said. "I've talked broad Yorkshire again like Mrs. Medlock said I mustn't. 'Nowt o' th' soart' means 'nothin'-of-the-sort,'" slowly and carefully, "but it takes so long to say it. Yorkshire's th' sunniest place on earth when it is sunny. I told thee tha'd like th' moor after a bit. Just you wait till you see th' gold-colored gorse blossoms an' th' blossoms o' th' broom, an' th' heather flowerin', all purple bells, an' hundreds o' butterflies flutterin' an' bees hummin' an' skylarks soarin' up an' singin'. You'll want to get out on it at sunrise an' live out on it all day like Dickon does."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Could I ever get there?" asked Mary wistfully, looking through her window at the far-off blue. It was so new and big and wonderful and such a heavenly color.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't know," answered Martha. "Tha's never used tha' legs since tha' was born, it seems to me. Tha' couldn't walk five mile. It's five mile to our cottage."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha stared at her a moment curiously before she took up her polishing brush and began to rub the grate again. She was thinking that the small plain face did not look quite as sour at this moment as it had done the first morning she saw it. It looked just a trifle like little Susan Ann's when she wanted something very much.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I'll ask my mother about it," she said. "She's one o' them that nearly always sees a way to do things. It's my day out today an' I'm goin' home. Eh! I am glad. Mrs. Medlock thinks a lot o' mother. Perhaps she could talk to her."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I should think tha' did," agreed Martha, polishing away.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She sat up on her heels again and rubbed the end of her nose with the back of her hand as if puzzled for a moment, but she ended quite positively.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, she's that sensible an' hard workin' an' good-natured an' clean that no one could help likin' her whether they'd seen her or not. When I'm goin' home to her on my day out I just jump for joy when I'm crossin' the moor."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I like Dickon," added Mary. "And I've never seen him."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well," said Martha stoutly, "I've told thee that th' very birds likes him an' th' rabbits an' wild sheep an' ponies, an' th' foxes themselves. I wonder," staring at her reflectively, "what Dickon would think of thee?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He wouldn't like me," said Mary in her stiff, cold little way. "No one does."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How does tha' like thysel'?" she inquired, really quite as if she were curious to know.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Not at all - really," she answered. "But I never thought of that before."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha grinned a little as if at some homely recollection.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Mother said that to me once," she said. "She was at her wash-tub an' I was in a bad temper an' talkin' ill of folk, an' she turns round on me an' says: 'Tha' young vixen, tha'! There tha' stands sayin' tha' doesn't like this one an' tha' doesn't like that one. How does tha' like thysel'?' It made me laugh an' it brought me to my senses in a minute."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She went away in high spirits as soon as she had given Mary her breakfast. She was going to walk five miles across the moor to the cottage, and she was going to help her mother with the washing and do the week's baking and enjoy herself thoroughly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Springtime's comin,'" he said. "Cannot tha' smell it?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I smell something nice and fresh and damp," she said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "That's th' good rich earth," he answered, digging away. "It's in a good humor makin' ready to grow things. It's glad when plantin' time comes. It's dull in th' winter when it's got nowt to do. In th' flower gardens out there things will be stirrin' down below in th' dark. Th' sun's warmin' 'em. You'll see bits o' green spikes stickin' out o' th' black earth after a bit."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Crocuses an' snowdrops an' daffydowndillys. Has tha' never seen them?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No. Everything is hot, and wet, and green after the rains in India," said Mary. "And I think things grow up in a night."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "These won't grow up in a night," said Weatherstaff. "Tha'll have to wait for 'em. They'll poke up a bit higher here, an' push out a spike more there, an' uncurl a leaf this day an' another that. You watch 'em."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Very soon she heard the soft rustling flight of wings again and she knew at once that the robin had come again. He was very pert and lively, and hopped about so close to her feet, and put his head on one side and looked at her so slyly that she asked Ben Weatherstaff a question.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Remembers thee!" said Weatherstaff indignantly. "He knows every cabbage stump in th' gardens, let alone th' people. He's never seen a little wench here before, an' he's bent on findin' out all about thee. Tha's no need to try to hide anything from him."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Are things stirring down below in the dark in that garden where he lives?" Mary inquired.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What garden?" grunted Weatherstaff, becoming surly again.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "The one where the old rose-trees are." She could not help asking, because she wanted so much to know. "Are all the flowers dead, or do some of them come again in the summer? Are there ever any roses?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Ask him," said Ben Weatherstaff, hunching his shoulders toward the robin. "He's the only one as knows. No one else has seen inside it for ten year'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Ten years was a long time, Mary thought. She had been born ten years ago.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She walked away, slowly thinking. She had begun to like the garden just as she had begun to like the robin and Dickon and Martha's mother. She was beginning to like Martha, too. That seemed a good many people to like - when you were not used to liking. She thought of the robin as one of the people. She went to her walk outside the long, ivy-covered wall over which she could see the tree-tops; and the second time she walked up and down the most interesting and exciting thing happened to her, and it was all through Ben Weatherstaff's robin.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She heard a chirp and a twitter, and when she looked at the bare flower-bed at her left side there he was hopping about and pretending to peck things out of the earth to persuade her that he had not followed her. But she knew he had followed her and the surprise so filled her with delight that she almost trembled a little.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You do remember me!" she cried out. "You do! You are prettier than anything else in the world!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She chirped, and talked, and coaxed and he hopped, and flirted his tail and twittered. It was as if he were talking. His red waistcoat was like satin and he puffed his tiny breast out and was so fine and so grand and so pretty that it was really as if he were showing her how important and like a human person a robin could be. Mistress Mary forgot that she had ever been contrary in her life when he allowed her to draw closer and closer to him, and bend down and talk and try to make something like robin sounds.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Oh! to think that he should actually let her come as near to him as that! He knew nothing in the world would make her put out her hand toward him or startle him in the least tiniest way. He knew it because he was a real person - only nicer than any other person in the world. She was so happy that she scarcely dared to breathe.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The flower-bed was not quite bare. It was bare of flowers because the perennial plants had been cut down for their winter rest, but there were tall shrubs and low ones which grew together at the back of the bed, and as the robin hopped about under them she saw him hop over a small pile of freshly turned up earth. He stopped on it to look for a worm. The earth had been turned up because a dog had been trying to dig up a mole and he had scratched quite a deep hole.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary looked at it, not really knowing why the hole was there, and as she looked she saw something almost buried in the newly-turned soil. It was something like a ring of rusty iron or brass and when the robin flew up into a tree nearby she put out her hand and picked the ring up. It was more than a ring, however; it was an old key which looked as if it had been buried a long time.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mistress Mary stood up and looked at it with an almost frightened face as it hung from her finger.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Perhaps it has been buried for ten years," she said in a whisper. "Perhaps it is the key to the garden!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Living as it were, all by herself in a house with a hundred mysteriously closed rooms and having nothing whatever to do to amuse herself, had set her inactive brain to working and was actually awakening her imagination. There is no doubt that the fresh, strong, pure air from the moor had a great deal to do with it. Just as it had given her an appetite, and fighting with the wind had stirred her blood, so the same things had stirred her mind. In India she had always been too hot and languid and weak to care much about anything, but in this place she was beginning to care and to want to do new things. Already she felt less "contrary," though she did not know why.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mrs. Medlock had allowed Martha to sleep all night at the cottage, but she was back at her work in the morning with cheeks redder than ever and in the best of spirits.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I got up at four o'clock," she said. "Eh! it was pretty on th' moor with th' birds gettin' up an' th' rabbits scamperin' about an' th' sun risin'. I didn't walk all th' way. A man gave me a ride in his cart an' I did enjoy myself."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She was full of stories of the delights of her day out. Her mother had been glad to see her and they had got the baking and washing all out of the way. She had even made each of the children a doughcake with a bit of brown sugar in it.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I had 'em all pipin' hot when they came in from playin' on th' moor. An' th' cottage all smelt o' nice, clean hot bakin' an' there was a good fire, an' they just shouted for joy. Our Dickon he said our cottage was good enough for a king to live in."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: In the evening they had all sat round the fire, and Martha and her mother had sewed patches on torn clothes and mended stockings and Martha had told them about the little girl who had come from India and who had been waited on all her life by what Martha called "blacks" until she didn't know how to put on her own stockings.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! they did like to hear about you," said Martha. "They wanted to know all about th' blacks an' about th' ship you came in. I couldn't tell 'em enough."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I'll tell you a great deal more before your next day out," she said, "so that you will have more to talk about. I dare say they would like to hear about riding on elephants and camels, and about the officers going to hunt tigers."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "My word!" cried delighted Martha. "It would set 'em clean off their heads. Would tha' really do that, Miss? It would be same as a wild beast show like we heard they had in York once."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "India is quite different from Yorkshire," Mary said slowly, as she thought the matter over. "I never thought of that. Did Dickon and your mother like to hear you talk about me?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't want a governess," said Mary sharply.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "But mother says you ought to be learnin' your book by this time an' you ought to have a woman to look after you, an' she says: 'Now, Martha, you just think how you'd feel yourself, in a big place like that, wanderin' about all alone, an' no mother. You do your best to cheer her up,' she says, an' I said I would."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You do cheer me up," she said. "I like to hear you talk."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Presently Martha went out of the room and came back with something held in her hands under her apron.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What does tha' think," she said, with a cheerful grin. "I've brought thee a present."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "A present!" exclaimed Mistress Mary. How could a cottage full of fourteen hungry people give anyone a present!
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "A man was drivin' across the moor peddlin'," Martha explained. "An' he stopped his cart at our door. He had pots an' pans an' odds an' ends, but mother had no money to buy anythin'. Just as he was goin' away our 'Lizabeth Ellen called out, 'Mother, he's got skippin'-ropes with red an' blue handles.' An' mother she calls out quite sudden, 'Here, stop, mister! How much are they?' An' he says 'Tuppence', an' mother she began fumblin' in her pocket an' she says to me, 'Martha, tha's brought me thy wages like a good lass, an' I've got four places to put every penny, but I'm just goin' to take tuppence out of it to buy that child a skippin'-rope,' an' she bought one an' here it is."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She brought it out from under her apron and exhibited it quite proudly. It was a strong, slender rope with a striped red and blue handle at each end, but Mary Lennox had never seen a skipping-rope before. She gazed at it with a mystified expression.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "For!" cried out Martha. "Does tha' mean that they've not got skippin'-ropes in India, for all they've got elephants and tigers and camels! No wonder most of 'em's black. This is what it's for; just watch me."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And she ran into the middle of the room and, taking a handle in each hand, began to skip, and skip, and skip, while Mary turned in her chair to stare at her, and the queer faces in the old portraits seemed to stare at her, too, and wonder what on earth this common little cottager had the impudence to be doing under their very noses. But Martha did not even see them. The interest and curiosity in Mistress Mary's face delighted her, and she went on skipping and counted as she skipped until she had reached a hundred.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I could skip longer than that," she said when she stopped. "I've skipped as much as five hundred when I was twelve, but I wasn't as fat then as I am now, an' I was in practice."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary got up from her chair beginning to feel excited herself.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It looks nice," she said. "Your mother is a kind woman. Do you think I could ever skip like that?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was plain that there was not a great deal of strength in Mistress Mary's arms and legs when she first began to skip. She was not very clever at it, but she liked it so much that she did not want to stop.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Put on tha' things and run an' skip out o' doors," said Martha. "Mother said I must tell you to keep out o' doors as much as you could, even when it rains a bit, so as tha' wrap up warm."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary put on her coat and hat and took her skipping-rope over her arm. She opened the door to go out, and then suddenly thought of something and turned back rather slowly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Martha," she said, "they were your wages. It was your two-pence really. Thank you." She said it stiffly because she was not used to thanking people or noticing that they did things for her. "Thank you," she said, and held out her hand because she did not know what else to do.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha gave her hand a clumsy little shake, as if she was not accustomed to this sort of thing either. Then she laughed.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh! th' art a queer, old-womanish thing," she said. "If tha'd been our 'Lizabeth Ellen tha'd have given me a kiss."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Nay, not me," she answered. "If tha' was different, p'raps tha'd want to thysel'. But tha' isn't. Run off outside an' play with thy rope."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well!" he exclaimed. "Upon my word. P'raps tha' art a young 'un, after all, an' p'raps tha's got child's blood in thy veins instead of sour buttermilk. Tha's skipped red into thy cheeks as sure as my name's Ben Weatherstaff. I wouldn't have believed tha' could do it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I never skipped before," Mary said. "I'm just beginning. I can only go up to twenty."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha' keep on," said Ben. "Tha' shapes well enough at it for a young 'un that's lived with heathen. Just see how he's watchin' thee," jerking his head toward the robin. "He followed after thee yesterday. He'll be at it again today. He'll be bound to find out what th' skippin'-rope is. He's never seen one. Eh!" shaking his head at the bird, "tha' curiosity will be th' death of thee sometime if tha' doesn't look sharp."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "You showed me where the key was yesterday," she said. "You ought to show me the door today; but I don't believe you know!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The robin flew from his swinging spray of ivy on to the top of the wall and he opened his beak and sang a loud, lovely trill, merely to show off. Nothing in the world is quite as adorably lovely as a robin when he shows off - and they are nearly always doing it.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary Lennox had heard a great deal about Magic in her Ayah's stories, and she always said that what happened almost at that moment was Magic.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: One of the nice little gusts of wind rushed down the walk, and it was a stronger one than the rest. It was strong enough to wave the branches of the trees, and it was more than strong enough to sway the trailing sprays of untrimmed ivy hanging from the wall. Mary had stepped close to the robin, and suddenly the gust of wind swung aside some loose ivy trails, and more suddenly still she jumped toward it and caught it in her hand. This she did because she had seen something under it - a round knob which had been covered by the leaves hanging over it. It was the knob of a door.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She put her hands under the leaves and began to pull and push them aside. Thick as the ivy hung, it nearly all was a loose and swinging curtain, though some had crept over wood and iron. Mary's heart began to thump and her hands to shake a little in her delight and excitement. The robin kept singing and twittering away and tilting his head on one side, as if he were as excited as she was. What was this under her hands which was square and made of iron and which her fingers found a hole in?
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was the lock of the door which had been closed ten years and she put her hand in her pocket, drew out the key and found it fitted the keyhole. She put the key in and turned it. It took two hands to do it, but it did turn.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And then she took a long breath and looked behind her up the long walk to see if anyone was coming. No one was coming. No one ever did come, it seemed, and she took another long breath, because she could not help it, and she held back the swinging curtain of ivy and pushed back the door which opened slowly - slowly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Then she slipped through it, and shut it behind her, and stood with her back against it, looking about her and breathing quite fast with excitement, and wonder, and delight.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How still it is!" she whispered. "How still!"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Then she waited a moment and listened at the stillness. The robin, who had flown to his treetop, was still as all the rest. He did not even flutter his wings; he sat without stirring, and looked at Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No wonder it is still," she whispered again. "I am the first person who has spoken in here for ten years."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She moved away from the door, stepping as softly as if she were afraid of awakening someone. She was glad that there was grass under her feet and that her steps made no sounds. She walked under one of the fairy-like gray arches between the trees and looked up at the sprays and tendrils which formed them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I wonder if they are all quite dead," she said. "Is it all a quite dead garden? I wish it wasn't."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: If she had been Ben Weatherstaff she could have told whether the wood was alive by looking at it, but she could only see that there were only gray or brown sprays and branches and none showed any signs of even a tiny leaf-bud anywhere.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But she was inside the wonderful garden and she could come through the door under the ivy any time and she felt as if she had found a world all her own.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Her skipping-rope had hung over her arm when she came in and after she had walked about for a while she thought she would skip round the whole garden, stopping when she wanted to look at things. There seemed to have been grass paths here and there, and in one or two corners there were alcoves of evergreen with stone seats or tall moss-covered flower urns in them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: As she came near the second of these alcoves she stopped skipping. There had once been a flowerbed in it, and she thought she saw something sticking out of the black earth - some sharp little pale green points. She remembered what Ben Weatherstaff had said and she knelt down to look at them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Yes, they are tiny growing things and they might be crocuses or snowdrops or daffodils," she whispered.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She bent very close to them and sniffed the fresh scent of the damp earth. She liked it very much.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Perhaps there are some other ones coming up in other places," she said. "I will go all over the garden and look."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She did not skip, but walked. She went slowly and kept her eyes on the ground. She looked in the old border beds and among the grass, and after she had gone round, trying to miss nothing, she had found ever so many more sharp, pale green points, and she had become quite excited again.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It isn't a quite dead garden," she cried out softly to herself. "Even if the roses are dead, there are other things alive."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She did not know anything about gardening, but the grass seemed so thick in some of the places where the green points were pushing their way through that she thought they did not seem to have room enough to grow. She searched about until she found a rather sharp piece of wood and knelt down and dug and weeded out the weeds and grass until she made nice little clear places around them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Now they look as if they could breathe," she said, after she had finished with the first ones. "I am going to do ever so many more. I'll do all I can see. If I haven't time today I can come tomorrow."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She went from place to place, and dug and weeded, and enjoyed herself so immensely that she was led on from bed to bed and into the grass under the trees. The exercise made her so warm that she first threw her coat off, and then her hat, and without knowing it she was smiling down on to the grass and the pale green points all the time.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The robin was tremendously busy. He was very much pleased to see gardening begun on his own estate. He had often wondered at Ben Weatherstaff. Where gardening is done all sorts of delightful things to eat are turned up with the soil. Now here was this new kind of creature who was not half Ben's size and yet had had the sense to come into his garden and begin at once.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mistress Mary worked in her garden until it was time to go to her midday dinner. In fact, she was rather late in remembering, and when she put on her coat and hat, and picked up her skipping-rope, she could not believe that she had been working two or three hours. She had been actually happy all the time; and dozens and dozens of the tiny, pale green points were to be seen in cleared places, looking twice as cheerful as they had looked before when the grass and weeds had been smothering them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I shall come back this afternoon," she said, looking all round at her new kingdom, and speaking to the trees and the rose-bushes as if they heard her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Then she ran lightly across the grass, pushed open the slow old door and slipped through it under the ivy. She had such red cheeks and such bright eyes and ate such a dinner that Martha was delighted.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Two pieces o' meat an' two helps o' rice puddin'!" she said. "Eh! mother will be pleased when I tell her what th' skippin'-rope's done for thee."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: In the course of her digging with her pointed stick Mistress Mary had found herself digging up a sort of white root rather like an onion. She had put it back in its place and patted the earth carefully down on it and just now she wondered if Martha could tell her what it was.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Martha," she said, "what are those white roots that look like onions?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "They're bulbs," answered Martha. "Lots o' spring flowers grow from 'em. Th' very little ones are snowdrops an' crocuses an' th' big ones are narcissuses an' jonquils and daffydowndillys. Th' biggest of all is lilies an' purple flags. Eh! they are nice. Dickon's got a whole lot of 'em planted in our bit o' garden."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Does Dickon know all about them?" asked Mary, a new idea taking possession of her.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Our Dickon can make a flower grow out of a brick walk. Mother says he just whispers things out o' th' ground."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Do bulbs live a long time? Would they live years and years if no one helped them?" inquired Mary anxiously.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "They're things as helps themselves," said Martha. "That's why poor folk can afford to have 'em. If you don't trouble 'em, most of 'em'll work away underground for a lifetime an' spread out an' have little 'uns. There's a place in th' park woods here where there's snowdrops by thousands. They're the prettiest sight in Yorkshire when th' spring comes. No one knows when they was first planted."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I wish the spring was here now," said Mary. "I want to see all the things that grow in England."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She had finished her dinner and gone to her favorite seat on the hearth-rug.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I wish - I wish I had a little spade," she said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Whatever does tha' want a spade for?" asked Martha, laughing. "Art tha' goin' to take to diggin'? I must tell mother that, too."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary looked at the fire and pondered a little. She must be careful if she meant to keep her secret kingdom. She wasn't doing any harm, but if Mr. Craven found out about the open door he would be fearfully angry and get a new key and lock it up forevermore. She really could not bear that.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "This is such a big lonely place," she said slowly, as if she were turning matters over in her mind. "The house is lonely, and the park is lonely, and the gardens are lonely. So many places seem shut up. I never did many things in India, but there were more people to look at - natives and soldiers marching by - and sometimes bands playing, and my Ayah told me stories. There is no one to talk to here except you and Ben Weatherstaff. And you have to do your work and Ben Weatherstaff won't speak to me often. I thought if I had a little spade I could dig somewhere as he does, and I might make a little garden if he would give me some seeds."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There now!" she exclaimed, "if that wasn't one of th' things mother said. She says, 'There's such a lot o' room in that big place, why don't they give her a bit for herself, even if she doesn't plant nothin' but parsley an' radishes? She'd dig an' rake away an' be right down happy over it.' Them was the very words she said."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Were they?" said Mary. "How many things she knows, doesn't she?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How much would a spade cost - a little one?" Mary asked.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well," was Martha's reflective answer, "at Thwaite village there's a shop or so an' I saw little garden sets with a spade an' a rake an' a fork all tied together for two shillings. An' they was stout enough to work with, too."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I've got more than that in my purse," said Mary. "Mrs. Morrison gave me five shillings and Mrs. Medlock gave me some money from Mr. Craven."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Did he remember thee that much?" exclaimed Martha.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Mrs. Medlock said I was to have a shilling a week to spend. She gives me one every Saturday. I didn't know what to spend it on."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "My word! that's riches," said Martha. "Tha' can buy anything in th' world tha' wants. Th' rent of our cottage is only one an' threepence an' it's like pullin' eye-teeth to get it. Now I've just thought of somethin'," putting her hands on her hips.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "In the shop at Thwaite they sell packages o' flower-seeds for a penny each, and our Dickon he knows which is th' prettiest ones an' how to make 'em grow. He walks over to Thwaite many a day just for th' fun of it. Does tha' know how to print letters?" suddenly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Our Dickon can only read printin'. If tha' could print we could write a letter to him an' ask him to go an' buy th' garden tools an' th' seeds at th' same time."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Oh! you're a good girl!" Mary cried. "You are, really! I didn't know you were so nice. I know I can print letters if I try. Let's ask Mrs. Medlock for a pen and ink and some paper."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I've got some of my own," said Martha. "I bought 'em so I could print a bit of a letter to mother of a Sunday. I'll go and get it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She ran out of the room, and Mary stood by the fire and twisted her thin little hands together with sheer pleasure.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "If I have a spade," she whispered, "I can make the earth nice and soft and dig up weeds. If I have seeds and can make flowers grow the garden won't be dead at all - it will come alive."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: This comes hoping to find you well as it leaves me at present. Miss Mary has plenty of money and will you go to Thwaite and buy her some flower seeds and a set of garden tools to make a flower-bed. Pick the prettiest ones and easy to grow because she has never done it before and lived in India which is different. Give my love to mother and everyone of you. Miss Mary is going to tell me a lot more so that on my next day out you can hear about elephants and camels and gentlemen going hunting lions and tigers.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "We'll put the money in th' envelope an' I'll get th' butcher boy to take it in his cart. He's a great friend o' Dickon's," said Martha.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How shall I get the things when Dickon buys them?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He'll bring 'em to you himself. He'll like to walk over this way."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Oh!" exclaimed Mary, "then I shall see him! I never thought I should see Dickon."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Does tha' want to see him?" asked Martha suddenly, for Mary had looked so pleased.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Yes, I do. I never saw a boy foxes and crows loved. I want to see him very much."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Martha gave a little start, as if she remembered something.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Now to think," she broke out, "to think o' me forgettin' that there; an' I thought I was goin' to tell you first thing this mornin'. I asked mother - and she said she'd ask Mrs. Medlock her own self."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What I said Tuesday. Ask her if you might be driven over to our cottage some day and have a bit o' mother's hot oat cake, an' butter, an' a glass o' milk."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It seemed as if all the interesting things were happening in one day. To think of going over the moor in the daylight and when the sky was blue! To think of going into the cottage which held twelve children!
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Does she think Mrs. Medlock would let me go?" she asked, quite anxiously.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, she thinks she would. She knows what a tidy woman mother is and how clean she keeps the cottage."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "If I went I should see your mother as well as Dickon," said Mary, thinking it over and liking the idea very much. "She doesn't seem to be like the mothers in India."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Her work in the garden and the excitement of the afternoon ended by making her feel quiet and thoughtful. Martha stayed with her until tea-time, but they sat in comfortable quiet and talked very little. But just before Martha went downstairs for the tea-tray, Mary asked a question.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Martha," she said, "has the scullery-maid had the toothache again today?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Because when I waited so long for you to come back I opened the door and walked down the corridor to see if you were coming. And I heard that far-off crying again, just as we heard it the other night. There isn't a wind today, so you see it couldn't have been the wind."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh!" said Martha restlessly. "Tha' mustn't go walkin' about in corridors an' listenin'. Mr. Craven would be that there angry there's no knowin' what he'd do."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I wasn't listening," said Mary. "I was just waiting for you - and I heard it. That's three times."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "My word! There's Mrs. Medlock's bell," said Martha, and she almost ran out of the room.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's the strangest house anyone ever lived in," said Mary drowsily, as she dropped her head on the cushioned seat of the armchair near her. Fresh air, and digging, and skipping-rope had made her feel so comfortably tired that she fell asleep.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha'rt like th' robin," he said to her one morning when he lifted his head and saw her standing by him. "I never knows when I shall see thee or which side tha'll come from."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "That's like him," snapped Ben Weatherstaff. "Makin' up to th' women folk just for vanity an' flightiness. There's nothin' he wouldn't do for th' sake o' showin' off an' flirtin' his tail-feathers. He's as full o' pride as an egg's full o' meat."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He very seldom talked much and sometimes did not even answer Mary's questions except by a grunt, but this morning he said more than usual. He stood up and rested one hobnailed boot on the top of his spade while he looked her over.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How long has tha' been here?" he jerked out.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha's beginnin' to do Misselthwaite credit," he said. "Tha's a bit fatter than tha' was an' tha's not quite so yeller. Tha' looked like a young plucked crow when tha' first came into this garden. Thinks I to myself I never set eyes on an uglier, sourer faced young 'un."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary was not vain and as she had never thought much of her looks she was not greatly disturbed.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I know I'm fatter," she said. "My stockings are getting tighter. They used to make wrinkles. There's the robin, Ben Weatherstaff."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: There, indeed, was the robin, and she thought he looked nicer than ever. His red waistcoat was as glossy as satin and he flirted his wings and tail and tilted his head and hopped about with all sorts of lively graces. He seemed determined to make Ben Weatherstaff admire him. But Ben was sarcastic.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, there tha' art!" he said. "Tha' can put up with me for a bit sometimes when tha's got no one better. Tha's been reddenin' up thy waistcoat an' polishin' thy feathers this two weeks. I know what tha's up to. Tha's courtin' some bold young madam somewhere tellin' thy lies to her about bein' th' finest cock robin on Missel Moor an' ready to fight all th' rest of 'em."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The robin was evidently in a fascinating, bold mood. He hopped closer and closer and looked at Ben Weatherstaff more and more engagingly. He flew on to the nearest currant bush and tilted his head and sang a little song right at him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha' thinks tha'll get over me by doin' that," said Ben, wrinkling his face up in such a way that Mary felt sure he was trying not to look pleased. "Tha' thinks no one can stand out against thee - that's what tha' thinks."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The robin spread his wings - Mary could scarcely believe her eyes. He flew right up to the handle of Ben Weatherstaff's spade and alighted on the top of it. Then the old man's face wrinkled itself slowly into a new expression. He stood still as if he were afraid to breathe - as if he would not have stirred for the world, lest his robin should start away. He spoke quite in a whisper.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, I'm danged!" he said as softly as if he were saying something quite different. "Tha' does know how to get at a chap - tha' does! Tha's fair unearthly, tha's so knowin'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And he stood without stirring - almost without drawing his breath - until the robin gave another flirt to his wings and flew away. Then he stood looking at the handle of the spade as if there might be Magic in it, and then he began to dig again and said nothing for several minutes.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: But because he kept breaking into a slow grin now and then, Mary was not afraid to talk to him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "No. I'm bachelder an' lodge with Martin at th' gate."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "If you had one," said Mary, "what would you plant?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "But if you wanted to make a flower garden," persisted Mary, "what would you plant?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Bulbs an' sweet-smellin' things - but mostly roses."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Ben Weatherstaff rooted up a weed and threw it aside before he answered.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, yes, I do. I was learned that by a young lady I was gardener to. She had a lot in a place she was fond of, an' she loved 'em like they was children - or robins. I've seen her bend over an' kiss 'em." He dragged out another weed and scowled at it. "That were as much as ten year' ago."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Where is she now?" asked Mary, much interested.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Heaven," he answered, and drove his spade deep into the soil, "'cording to what parson says."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "What happened to the roses?" Mary asked again, more interested than ever.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Did they quite die? Do roses quite die when they are left to themselves?" she ventured.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well, I'd got to like 'em - an' I liked her - an' she liked 'em," Ben Weatherstaff admitted reluctantly. "Once or twice a year I'd go an' work at 'em a bit - prune 'em an' dig about th' roots. They run wild, but they was in rich soil, so some of 'em lived."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "When they have no leaves and look gray and brown and dry, how can you tell whether they are dead or alive?" inquired Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Wait till th' spring gets at 'em - wait till th' sun shines on th' rain and th' rain falls on th' sunshine an' then tha'll find out."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "How - how?" cried Mary, forgetting to be careful.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Look along th' twigs an' branches an' if tha' see a bit of a brown lump swelling here an' there, watch it after th' warm rain an' see what happens." He stopped suddenly and looked curiously at her eager face. "Why does tha' care so much about roses an' such, all of a sudden?" he demanded.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mistress Mary felt her face grow red. She was almost afraid to answer.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I - I want to play that - that I have a garden of my own," she stammered. "I - there is nothing for me to do. I have nothing - and no one."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Well," said Ben Weatherstaff slowly, as he watched her, "that's true. Tha' hasn't."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He said it in such an odd way that Mary wondered if he was actually a little sorry for her. She had never felt sorry for herself; she had only felt tired and cross, because she disliked people and things so much. But now the world seemed to be changing and getting nicer. If no one found out about the secret garden, she should enjoy herself always.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She stayed with him for ten or fifteen minutes longer and asked him as many questions as she dared. He answered everyone of them in his queer grunting way and he did not seem really cross and did not pick up his spade and leave her. He said something about roses just as she was going away and it reminded her of the ones he had said he had been fond of.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Do you go and see those other roses now?" she asked.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Not been this year. My rheumatics has made me too stiff in th' joints."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He said it in his grumbling voice, and then quite suddenly he seemed to get angry with her, though she did not see why he should.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Now look here!" he said sharply. "Don't tha' ask so many questions. Tha'rt th' worst wench for askin' questions I've ever come across. Get thee gone an' play thee. I've done talkin' for today."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And he said it so crossly that she knew there was not the least use in staying another minute. She went skipping slowly down the outside walk, thinking him over and saying to herself that, queer as it was, here was another person whom she liked in spite of his crossness. She liked old Ben Weatherstaff. Yes, she did like him. She always wanted to try to make him talk to her. Also she began to believe that he knew everything in the world about flowers.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: There was a laurel-hedged walk which curved round the secret garden and ended at a gate which opened into a wood, in the park. She thought she would slip round this walk and look into the wood and see if there were any rabbits hopping about. She enjoyed the skipping very much and when she reached the little gate she opened it and went through because she heard a low, peculiar whistling sound and wanted to find out what it was.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: When he saw Mary he held up his hand and spoke to her in a voice almost as low as and rather like his piping.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Don't tha' move," he said. "It'd flight 'em."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary remained motionless. He stopped playing his pipe and began to rise from the ground. He moved so slowly that it scarcely seemed as though he were moving at all, but at last he stood on his feet and then the squirrel scampered back up into the branches of his tree, the pheasant withdrew his head and the rabbits dropped on all fours and began to hop away, though not at all as if they were frightened.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I'm Dickon," the boy said. "I know tha'rt Miss Mary."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Then Mary realized that somehow she had known at first that he was Dickon. Who else could have been charming rabbits and pheasants as the natives charm snakes in India? He had a wide, red, curving mouth and his smile spread all over his face.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I got up slow," he explained, "because if tha' makes a quick move it startles 'em. A body 'as to move gentle an' speak low when wild things is about."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He did not speak to her as if they had never seen each other before but as if he knew her quite well. Mary knew nothing about boys and she spoke to him a little stiffly because she felt rather shy.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He stooped to pick up something which had been lying on the ground beside him when he piped.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I've got th' garden tools. There's a little spade an' rake an' a fork an' hoe. Eh! they are good 'uns. There's a trowel, too. An' th' woman in th' shop threw in a packet o' white poppy an' one o' blue larkspur when I bought th' other seeds."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She wished she could talk as he did. His speech was so quick and easy. It sounded as if he liked her and was not the least afraid she would not like him, though he was only a common moor boy, in patched clothes and with a funny face and a rough, rusty-red head. As she came closer to him she noticed that there was a clean fresh scent of heather and grass and leaves about him, almost as if he were made of them. She liked it very much and when she looked into his funny face with the red cheeks and round blue eyes she forgot that she had felt shy.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Let us sit down on this log and look at them," she said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: They sat down and he took a clumsy little brown paper package out of his coat pocket. He untied the string and inside there were ever so many neater and smaller packages with a picture of a flower on each one.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "There's a lot o' mignonette an' poppies," he said. "Mignonette's th' sweetest smellin' thing as grows, an' it'll grow wherever you cast it, same as poppies will. Them as'll come up an' bloom if you just whistle to 'em, them's th' nicest of all."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He stopped and turned his head quickly, his poppy-cheeked face lighting up.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Where's that robin as is callin' us?" he said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: The chirp came from a thick holly bush, bright with scarlet berries, and Mary thought she knew whose it was.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye," said Dickon, as if it was the most natural thing in the world, "he's callin' someone he's friends with. That's same as sayin' 'Here I am. Look at me. I wants a bit of a chat.' There he is in the bush. Whose is he?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He's Ben Weatherstaff's, but I think he knows me a little," answered Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, he knows thee," said Dickon in his low voice again. "An' he likes thee. He's took thee on. He'll tell me all about thee in a minute."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He moved quite close to the bush with the slow movement Mary had noticed before, and then he made a sound almost like the robin's own twitter. The robin listened a few seconds, intently, and then answered quite as if he were replying to a question.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Aye, he's a friend o' yours," chuckled Dickon.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Do you think he is?" cried Mary eagerly. She did so want to know. "Do you think he really likes me?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "He wouldn't come near thee if he didn't," answered Dickon. "Birds is rare choosers an' a robin can flout a body worse than a man. See, he's making up to thee now. 'Cannot tha' see a chap?' he's sayin'."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: And it really seemed as if it must be true. He so sidled and twittered and tilted as he hopped on his bush.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Do you understand everything birds say?" said Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Dickon's grin spread until he seemed all wide, red, curving mouth, and he rubbed his rough head.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I think I do, and they think I do," he said. "I've lived on th' moor with 'em so long. I've watched 'em break shell an' come out an' fledge an' learn to fly an' begin to sing, till I think I'm one of 'em. Sometimes I think p'raps I'm a bird, or a fox, or a rabbit, or a squirrel, or even a beetle, an' I don't know it."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: He laughed and came back to the log and began to talk about the flower seeds again. He told her what they looked like when they were flowers; he told her how to plant them, and watch them, and feed and water them.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "See here," he said suddenly, turning round to look at her. "I'll plant them for thee myself. Where is tha' garden?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mary's thin hands clutched each other as they lay on her lap. She did not know what to say, so for a whole minute she said nothing. She had never thought of this. She felt miserable. And she felt as if she went red and then pale.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Tha's got a bit o' garden, hasn't tha'?" Dickon said.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: It was true that she had turned red and then pale. Dickon saw her do it, and as she still said nothing, he began to be puzzled.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Wouldn't they give thee a bit?" he asked. "Hasn't tha' got any yet?"
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She held her hands tighter and turned her eyes toward him.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't know anything about boys," she said slowly. "Could you keep a secret, if I told you one? It's a great secret. I don't know what I should do if anyone found it out. I believe I should die!" She said the last sentence quite fiercely.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Dickon looked more puzzled than ever and even rubbed his hand over his rough head again, but he answered quite good-humoredly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I'm keepin' secrets all th' time," he said. "If I couldn't keep secrets from th' other lads, secrets about foxes' cubs, an' birds' nests, an' wild things' holes, there'd be naught safe on th' moor. Aye, I can keep secrets."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mistress Mary did not mean to put out her hand and clutch his sleeve but she did it.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I've stolen a garden," she said very fast. "It isn't mine. It isn't anybody's. Nobody wants it, nobody cares for it, nobody ever goes into it. Perhaps everything is dead in it already. I don't know."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She began to feel hot and as contrary as she had ever felt in her life.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I don't care, I don't care! Nobody has any right to take it from me when I care about it and they don't. They're letting it die, all shut in by itself," she ended passionately, and she threw her arms over her face and burst out crying - poor little Mistress Mary.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Dickon's curious blue eyes grew rounder and rounder.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh-h-h!" he said, drawing his exclamation out slowly, and the way he did it meant both wonder and sympathy.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "I've nothing to do," said Mary. "Nothing belongs to me. I found it myself and I got into it myself. I was only just like the robin, and they wouldn't take it from the robin."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Where is it?" asked Dickon in a dropped voice.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Mistress Mary got up from the log at once. She knew she felt contrary again, and obstinate, and she did not care at all. She was imperious and Indian, and at the same time hot and sorrowful.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: She led him round the laurel path and to the walk where the ivy grew so thickly. Dickon followed her with a queer, almost pitying, look on his face. He felt as if he were being led to look at some strange bird's nest and must move softly. When she stepped to the wall and lifted the hanging ivy he started. There was a door and Mary pushed it slowly open and they passed in together, and then Mary stood and waved her hand round defiantly.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "It's this," she said. "It's a secret garden, and I'm the only one in the world who wants it to be alive."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: Dickon looked round and round about it, and round and round again.
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett

quotes.text: "Eh!" he almost whispered, "it is a queer, pretty place! It's like as if a body was in a dream."
quotes.source: The Secret Garden — Frances Hodgson Burnett
